The dominant Morrison predator, known from dozens of individuals at the Cleveland-Lloyd quarry.
taxa.hb: terrestrial apex predator

taxa.note: Plated, spike-tailed, and with a brain famously small relative to its bulk.
taxa.hb: low browser with dorsal plates and a spiked tail

taxa.note: A shrew-sized docodont with complex grinding molars -- a side branch of the mammals that could chew as well as shear.
A three-metre, long-legged, fast plant-eater of the Morrison plains -- a gazelle among the giants.
One of the first ankylosaurs, three metres long, with a skull roof of fused armour and a body studded with cone-shaped spikes.
The culpeo, a fox-like South American canid of the Andes and the Patagonian steppe.
The Amazon river dolphin, pink-skinned and flexible enough to hunt in flooded forest.
Darwin's rhea, the flightless runner of Patagonian steppe and Andean puna.
One of the world's largest freshwater fish, an air-breather in oxygen-poor floodplain water.
The alerce, a giant cypress of the Valdivian rainforest; one tree is over 3,600 years old.
Frailejones, the woolly giant rosettes of the paramo, wrapped in their own dead leaves against nightly frost.
Pampas grass, three-metre tussocks with silver plumes.
A ground sloth the size of an elephant, rearing up to pull down branches.
taxa.hb: terrestrial browser, able to rear on its hindlimbs

taxa.note: A camel-bodied, trunk-nosed litoptern, one of the last of the endemic ungulates.
A glyptodont with a spiked tail-club, among the largest of the armoured Ice Age herbivores.
One of the endemic South American ungulate orders that the interchange extinguished.
taxa.hb: heavy grazer, rhinoceros-like in build but unrelated

taxa.note: Apex predators of isolated South America; possibly island-hopped north by ~5 Ma.
taxa.hb: flightless cursorial predator

taxa.note: The largest rodent known: a bull-sized relative of the pacarana from Uruguay, with incisors strong enough to be used like tusks.
A marsupial-relative sabre-tooth: South America's pouched answer to Smilodon, with canines that never stopped growing and bony scabbards on the jaw.
Car-sized armadillo relatives under a rigid dome of bone, some with a spiked tail club. They walked north to Florida and Arizona after the interchange.
The monkey puzzle of the southern Andes, a Jurassic-looking conifer that can live a thousand years.
The moriche palm, forming swamp stands across lowland tropical South America; its pollen marks the great Miocene wetland of western Amazonia.
The largest freshwater turtle ever, a side-neck with a shell over three metres across and horns on the front of it.
A slender-snouted gharial up to ten metres long, a specialised fish-eater sharing the water with the giant caimans.
The Brazil nut tree, a fifty-metre emergent that only one large bee can pollinate and only the agouti can plant.
A giant caiman over ten metres long, ruling the vast Pebas wetland of Miocene Amazonia.
Sun-pitcher plants trapping insects on nutrient-starved sandstone summits.
Paper-bark trees forming the highest true forests on Earth, above 4,000 m.
Ground sloths with pebbles of bone set in their skin. Mylodon's hide and dung survive in a Patagonian cave, fresh enough to have fooled explorers.
An ancient plant family largely confined to the shield, radiating on the tepui summits.
A 'terror bird' - a two-metre flightless predator that was a top carnivore of the Miocene pampas.
A tapir-like endemic ungulate of the Santa Cruz beds of Patagonia.
Rhino-sized South American natives with tusks and probably a short trunk -- nothing to do with elephants or tapirs, only convergent on them.
An endemic radiation of hundreds of snail and mussel species, found nowhere else, whose shells date the wetland bed by bed.
Still living - monkey puzzle and Norfolk Island pine are the same genus that dominated Jurassic forests.
taxa.hb: emergent canopy tree

taxa.note: An elephant-like endemic ungulate of the Oligocene Salla and Deseado faunas.
An endemic order of South American hoofed mammals that evolved in continental isolation.
Land-going crocodile relatives with deep skulls and serrated, dinosaur-like teeth, top predators in South America long after the dinosaurs.
The oldest known New World monkey, from Bolivia -- descended from African primates that had crossed the Atlantic, probably on floating vegetation.
Southern beech forest growing on Antarctica at high southern latitudes -- forest on a continent now under ice.
taxa.hb: canopy tree of cool temperate rainforest

taxa.note: A bear-sized sparassodont, a marsupial-line predator of the Oligocene with ever-growing canines.
The ground sloths that island-hopped: in the Caribbean by the Oligocene and in North America well before the land bridge; Megalonyx reached Alaska.
Rock tripe: leathery lichens clinging to bare rock, among the dominant visible life of ice-free polar and alpine ground.
A giant penguin, over 1.5 m tall, from the La Meseta beds before the ice arrived.
Horned tortoises with clubbed tails: a Gondwanan family that survived on Lord Howe Island and Vanuatu until people reached them.
Gum trees. Eucalypts and charcoal rise together through the Miocene record: fire and aridity remaking a rainforest continent. Their oldest fossils, oddly, are from Patagonia.
Gnawing, high-toothed mammals unique to the southern continents; Madagascar's Adalatherium shows they could reach the size of a badger.
Armadillos, the oldest surviving South American mammal lineage, and one of the few interchange migrants still pushing north.
Marsupials on Seymour Island, recording the old land connection between Antarctica, South America and Australia.
The grasses. Present from the Late Cretaceous, and ecologically almost invisible until about 40 Ma, when open grassland begins.
Tree ferns, with trunks to twenty metres, in wet forests from the Jurassic to the present; the pale forms of Cretaceous polar forests and of today's cloud forests alike.
Marsupial-relative carnivores that filled the cat-and-dog roles on the island continent.
A 13-metre snake from the Paleocene Cerrejon rainforest of Colombia - the largest snake known.
taxa.hb: semi-aquatic ambush predator

taxa.note: A car-sized side-necked turtle sharing Titanoboa's steamy post-impact wetlands.
The oldest neotropical rainforest known: palms, legumes and aroids in a structurally modern canopy only a few million years after the asteroid, and hot enough to support Titanoboa.
Lungless salamanders that breathe through their skin; the Appalachians hold their greatest diversity.
A weasel-sized early sparassodont, a climbing predator at the root of South America's marsupial-line carnivores.
A mouse-sized marsupial relative from the earliest Paleocene of Bolivia, found as groups of complete skeletons -- perhaps families killed together.
Lizard-like but not lizards. Worldwide in the Mesozoic; today one species, the tuatara, survives on New Zealand's offshore islands.
Palms. In the Eocene hothouse they grew at fifty degrees north beside crocodiles; their limit has been a frost line ever since.
A titanosaur about 26 metres long, known from a remarkably complete skeleton -- and still growing when it died.
A five-metre, long-snouted Patagonian raptor with small arms -- South America ran its own line of dromaeosaurs.
Stoneworts: green algae of clear fresh water that stand like tiny horsetails and coat themselves in lime; their oospores are the commonest plant fossil of ancient lake beds.
A small titanosaur studded with bony armour plates -- the discovery that showed sauropods could be armoured at all.
A four-metre elasmarian ornithopod with thin bony plates along its ribs -- one of a family of southern plant-eaters that reached Antarctica and Australia.
A horned, tiny-armed abelisaur theropod endemic to Cretaceous South America.
A deep-snouted land crocodyliform with blade-like teeth, one of the top predators of the Late Cretaceous of Brazil, where big theropods were scarce.
Short-faced predators with arms reduced almost to nothing: the top carnivores of the Cretaceous southern continents.
The last and largest sauropods, wide-hipped and often armoured. They are the big herbivores of every southern continent until the end of the Cretaceous.
A small Patagonian ornithopod known from many individuals, with gizzard stones still in its belly.
A six-metre abelisaurid with tiny arms and low bumps instead of horns, known from one of the most complete abelisaurid skeletons.
Land-living crocodile relatives of the southern continents: long-legged runners, some with mammal-like teeth, some plant-eaters.
Shearing-toothed Mesozoic mammals, the carnivores of their world -- including the one found with a dinosaur inside it.
A small, long-legged, dog-like crocodyliform that ran on land across Cretaceous Gondwana, found from Brazil and Niger to Patagonia.
A twelve-metre carcharodontosaurid; a bone bed of seven individuals of different ages hints that it hunted the giant sauropods in groups.
A titanosaur among the largest land animals ever, from the Cretaceous of Patagonia.
Crocodile-snouted, fish-eating theropods of river deltas and coasts.
A giant coelacanth of the rivers and lagoons of Gondwana -- up to five metres long and more, the largest coelacanth known.
A chicken-sized, long-snouted dromaeosaur of the southern unenlagiine branch, which probably caught small prey and fish.
A snake with a hip bone and working hind legs, from the Cenomanian of Patagonia -- evidence that snakes lost their legs on land, not in the sea.
A giant carcharodontosaur, rivalling T. rex in size, hunting the Patagonian titanosaurs.
Thirty-seven metres and some sixty tonnes: among the largest land animals known, from a single Patagonian quarry of six individuals.
A Brazilian pterosaur carrying a tall sail-like crest on a short, parrot-beaked skull.
A small coelurosaur, one of the few dinosaurs preserved with soft tissue -- muscle fibres and skin among its bones.
A spinosaurid with a long, crocodile-like fishing snout; its name records the irritation of scientists given a skull that fossil dealers had 'improved' with plaster.
A thalassodromid pterosaur with a five-metre wingspan and a tall, rounded head crest, from the lagoon beds of north-east Brazil.
The African elephant, and the reason the Afrotropical realm still has an intact large-mammal fauna when every other realm lost one.
The secretarybird, a long-legged raptor that hunts snakes on foot.
The spotted hyena: a hunter as much as a scavenger, living in female-led clans. Ice Age Europe had it too, as the cave hyena.
Africa keeps the intact big-mammal community - elephants, rhinos, hippos - that other continents lost.
A fungus farmed in gardens inside termite mounds -- an agriculture tens of millions of years older than our own.
The flat-topped thorn trees of African savanna, whose spread tracks the Miocene expansion of grassland.
The baobab, storing water in a massively swollen trunk -- the signature tree of seasonally arid Africa.
Sugarbushes: the emblem of the Cape fynbos, a fire-dependent heathland with more plant species than any rainforest of its size.
A moose-shaped giraffid with two pairs of horn-like ossicones, among the heaviest ruminants known.
The addax, an antelope that can live without drinking free water.
Associated with the earliest widely accepted stone tool industries, right at the interval's close.
A heavily-built, small-brained hominin of eastern Africa with huge grinding molars, sharing the early Pleistocene with the first members of Homo.
The quiver tree: a giant tree-aloe of the Namib edge, now dying back at the hot end of its range.
Small-brained, upright-walking hominins; the Laetoli trackway in Tanzania records them walking through volcanic ash 3.66 million years ago.
The fog-basking beetle, standing head-down to drink condensation off its own back.
Heavily armoured Tanganyikan snails that look marine, shaped by an arms race with shell-crushing crabs.
A two-leaved gymnosperm that lives a thousand years on fog alone.
Lucy's species: bipedal, small-brained, and the maker of the Laetoli footprint trail.
Mammoths spread across the newly cold northern continents as the mammoth steppe forms.
A proboscidean with downward-curving lower tusks, unrelated to any surviving elephant lineage.
A woodland hominin from Ethiopia that walked upright on the ground yet kept a grasping big toe for the trees.
Grasses using the C4 photosynthetic pathway, which is efficient in warm, dry, low-CO2 air. They build tropical savanna from about 8 Ma.
A late-Miocene Chadian hominin near the split of the human and chimpanzee lines.
Hippos: the closest living relatives of whales. Out of Africa in the late Miocene as far as Britain and Java; dwarf species lived on Madagascar and the Mediterranean islands.
African lungfish, surviving the dry season encased in mud.
A three-toed grazing horse whose rapid spread across the Old World is a datable event in its own right.
Screw pines on stilt roots, fringing Indo-Pacific shores.
An early African ape without a tail, near the base of the hominoid radiation.
taxa.hb: arboreal quadruped

taxa.note: Old World monkeys -- baboons, macaques, colobines. African until the late Miocene, then across Eurasia to Japan.
Swamp palms bearing the longest leaves of any plant, along the flooded interior.
Aardvarks: solitary termite-eaters with peg teeth, the only survivors of their order.
Mastodons: browsing proboscideans with cone-cusped teeth, a separate line from elephants and mammoths. The American mastodon lasted to the end of the Ice Age.
Four-tusked, long-jawed elephant relatives that walked out of Africa at about 19 Ma and eventually reached Patagonia.
Mangrove is the one forest that shows up as coastline rather than as interior vegetation, and it is a Cenozoic feature.
taxa.hb: intertidal tree on stilt roots, salt-excluding

taxa.note: A rhino-like herbivore with two enormous horns, endemic to the Fayum swamps.
An early Fayum proboscidean 2.5 m tall with short tusks in both jaws and the beginnings of a trunk.
A Fayum catarrhine near the base of the Old World monkey and ape split.
A hyrax as heavy as a small rhinoceros, the giant of the hyraxes that then held Africa's plant-eating niches.
Royal ferns, a genus so conservative that a Jurassic rhizome from Sweden is cell for cell like a living one.
Cyperaceae: grass-like plants of wet ground, marsh and tundra, where true grasses do less well.
A pig-sized, semi-aquatic early proboscidean - a distant, low-slung ancestor of elephants.
Fruit-eating birds -- hornbills, toucans, pigeons. Tropical trees largely depend on them to move seeds, so the forest needs them to regenerate.
Woody climbers using trees as scaffolding to reach the light. Like epiphytes, they exist only where there is a canopy.
Plants growing on other plants: orchids, bromeliads, ferns. They need a canopy to live in, so they date it.
Flowering trees closing a canopy overhead. That structure is what makes a rainforest a rainforest, and it does not exist before the Late Cretaceous.
A squirrel-monkey-sized early anthropoid of the Fayum, a leaper in the trees that fringed the Oligocene rivers.
Grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and large brains -- a group built by and largely confined to closed forest canopy.
An eighteen-metre fully aquatic archaeocete with vestigial hind limbs, preserved by the hundred at Wadi Al-Hitan.
taxa.hb: fully aquatic, serpentine, with vestigial hindlimbs

taxa.note: Brackish-water snails that radiated into dozens of endemic Lake Pannon species.
Springtails, among the first land animals -- Rhyniella from the Rhynie chert is Early Devonian -- and among the last to give up before the ice; they live in every soil on Earth.
The oldest known proboscidean: a fox-sized animal from the Paleocene of Morocco, 55 million years before the mammoths.
Sawflies first, then wasps, bees and ants. Their rise tracks the flowering plants they came to pollinate.
Southern conifers -- podocarps, rimu, totara -- that clothed warm-temperate Gondwana and still dominate many southern and tropical-mountain forests.
Mosses. They are most of Antarctica's land vegetation today, and beds of them lie freeze-dried in its Miocene tundra deposits.
The ginkgo lineage at its widest, in mid-latitude forests on nearly every continent. One species, Ginkgo biloba, is still alive.
Monkey-puzzle and kauri relatives: worldwide in the Mesozoic, southern-hemisphere survivors today.
A titanosaur of Campanian Egypt, the first good Late Cretaceous dinosaur from mainland Africa, whose kin link its fauna to Europe's.
A six-metre abelisaurid with a wrinkled, pitted face -- perhaps more a scavenger than a hunter.
The 'boar croc': a land-going crocodyliform with three pairs of tusk-like fangs and an armoured snout, perhaps for ramming.
A long-limbed, eight-metre theropod of the mid-Cretaceous river systems of North Africa -- a fast runner beside the fish-eating Spinosaurus.
A colossal titanosaur from the mangrove coasts of Late Cretaceous Egypt (Bahariya).
A titanosaur from the East African rift sediments, part of a distinct southern fauna.
Cycad-like plants with tight, flower-like cones that were probably insect pollinated. An independent Mesozoic run at the flower that left no descendants.
A shark-toothed giant predator of the mid-Cretaceous North African floodplains.
A sail-backed, semi-aquatic theropod larger than T. rex, from the Kem Kem rivers of the Sahara.
An azhdarchoid pterosaur with a straight, pointed, spear-like beak and a wingspan of about six metres.
A sail-backed, paddle-tailed theropod that hunted fish in North African river systems.
A sauropod with a vacuum-cleaner mouth: five hundred teeth along the square front edge of a featherweight skull, cropping plants at ground level.
A squat, heavy iguanodontian of Niger with a thumb spike and a body built low like a hippo's -- perhaps half-aquatic.
A sail-backed iguanodont sharing the lush Cretaceous river deltas of what is now the desert.
'SuperCroc': a twelve-metre, eight-tonne crocodile relative of the Cretaceous rivers of the Sahara and Brazil.
An eleven-metre spinosaur of the Sahara's Cretaceous rivers, with a long, narrow, fish-trap snout.
A carcharodontosaurid with a thick bony brow over each eye, an early relative of the giant Carcharodontosaurus.
An early titanosaur, one of the first known from a skull -- a clue to how the last great group of sauropods began.
A towering sauropod from Tanzania's Tendaguru beds, long described as an African species of Brachiosaurus before differences in its skull and proportions placed it in its own genus.
Robust Jurassic predators seven to ten metres long -- the family of the first dinosaur ever named.
A horned, blade-toothed predator that shared the Morrison plain with the larger Allosaurus.
A small, fast ornithopod found by the hundreds in one bone bed -- a herd of all ages killed together, perhaps by drought.
A short-necked sauropod with a double row of tall spines along its neck and back, which may have held up a ridge or sail.
Tendaguru's stegosaur: plates over the shoulders giving way to long paired spikes down the back and tail.
Red deer and their relatives, the characteristic large browsers of the Palearctic woodland and steppe.
The Caspian seal, stranded in an inland sea since the Paratethys broke up.
The Caucasian tur, a heavy-horned ibex found only on the Greater Caucasus.
The omul, the whitefish on which Lake Baikal's fishery has always rested.
The European larch, a deciduous conifer at the timberline.
Heather: the low evergreen shrub that makes the moorland of Atlantic Europe, on poor, acid, often burnt ground.
The nerpa, the world's only wholly freshwater seal, two thousand kilometres from the nearest sea.
Orangutans, the red apes of Borneo and Sumatra, once found north to China.
The crested ibis, down to seven birds in the Qinling foothills in 1981 and since recovered.
A branching green freshwater sponge forming metre-high underwater forests on Baikal's rocky slopes.
Armoured, spiny amphipods: part of a species flock of over 350 amphipods found only in Lake Baikal.
The Sulawesi kauri, a towering araucarian conifer tapped for dammar resin.
The silver fir of the European mountain forests.
The Siberian stone pine, whose nuts feed the taiga from nutcrackers to bears.
The Chinese giant salamander, up to 1.8 m, the largest living amphibian.
Toad-headed agamas, the small lizards of Central Asian sand and gravel desert up to 5,000 m.
A parasite with no leaves, stem or roots, producing the largest single flower on Earth, a metre across and smelling of carrion.
Tarsiers: tiny nocturnal primates with eyes each as large as their brain, and the only wholly carnivorous primates.
Killifish of salt springs and desert pools around the Mediterranean and Arabia, tolerant of brine saltier than the sea.
The timber bamboos of China, mass-flowering and dying back in cycles decades long.
Feather grasses whose awns drill their own seed into the soil.
A large Miocene ape from the Siwaliks, close to the ancestry of the orangutan.
An endemic brackish-water mussel that swarmed the isolated, freshening Paratethyan basins.
Tough, mat-forming sedges whose turf makes the vast alpine meadows of high Asia and the Arctic.
A small alligator relative, the common crocodilian of Europe's lakes and rivers from the Eocene to the Miocene.
Rhododendrons: evergreen shrubs and small trees that band wet mountain slopes by altitude, with their greatest diversity in the Sino-Himalaya.
A hornless rhinocerotoid five metres at the shoulder and around twenty tonnes -- the largest land mammal known.
A horse relative that looked more like a tapir, from pony- to horse-sized, which browsed the Eocene forests of Europe's islands.
An Asian brontothere with a tall bony 'battering ram' rising from its snout, hollow and perhaps used for calling.
Known from one 83 cm skull from Inner Mongolia: possibly the largest land-living carnivorous mammal, and a hoofed one.
A long-tailed, long-snouted insectivore that ran on its hind legs through the undergrowth of the Eocene forests of Europe.
A tiny early anthropoid from the Eocene of China, small enough to sit in a hand -- evidence that the monkey-and-ape line began in Asia.
A small Eocene browsing horse relative, found at Messel with leaves still in its stomach.
A squirrel-like early rodent nearly a metre long with its bushy tail, preserved at Messel with leaves in its gut.
An exquisitely complete Messel primate, gut contents and all, from near the base of the primate radiation.
An Eocene oil-shale lake in Germany preserving bats, early horses and gut contents in mirror detail.
A large flightless bird once assumed to be a predator, now thought to have been a heavy-billed herbivore; the same lineage also reached Ellesmere Island in Arctic Canada.
One of the earliest bats: its stomach contents show it hunted moths near the forest floor, and its ear bones show it could echolocate.
A hippo-like, tusked pantodont of the hothouse Eocene, found as far north as Ellesmere Island with a brain smaller than any mammal of its size.
The dog-sized ancestral horse, browsing in closed forest on four toes.
An early bat from Green River with fully modern wings and evidence of echolocation.
An early dinocerate from the Paleocene of Mongolia and China -- a tapir-sized ancestor of the horned, tusked uintatheres.
A bear-sized arctocyonid with blunt teeth and a heavy tail -- an omnivore of the Paleocene forests on both sides of the North Atlantic.
A small hoofed mammal of the Paleocene of France, known from hundreds of individuals in a single quarry.
A small gnawing mammal from the Paleocene of China, close to the common ancestor of rodents and rabbits.
A dog-sized pantodont of the earliest Paleocene of South China, one of the first mammals to take over the plant-eating roles the dinosaurs had left.
A wastebasket of archaic hoofed mammals from which most modern ungulate groups eventually emerge.
A giraffe-sized pterosaur from the Cretaceous island of Hateg in what is now Romania, apex predator of a dwarf-dinosaur fauna.
A small, primitive duckbill of the Hațeg island in the latest Cretaceous -- dwarfed, like much of the island's fauna, and a relic of an older lineage.
A pig-sized rhabdodontid, one of the dwarfed dinosaurs of the Hațeg island whose small size first suggested 'island dwarfing' to Baron Nopcsa a century ago.
A dwarf titanosaur of the Hațeg island, six metres long and about the weight of a horse -- a sauropod shrunk by island life.
Flowering plants go from rare to dominant inside forty million years, pulling pollinating insects, fruit-eating birds and the modern structure of forests along with them.
A stocky island paravian of Hațeg -- a dromaeosaur or a flightless bird -- with two big sickle claws on each foot.
The Asian giant tyrannosaur of the Nemegt Formation, close kin to T. rex and nearly as large.
A twelve-metre titanosaur known from a headless skeleton; its tail vertebrae suggest it could rear up on its tail like a tripod.
Known for fifty years only from its 2.4 m arms; the rest turned out to be a hump-backed, duck-billed giant ornithomimosaur.
Turkey-sized and feathered, from the Gobi -- one specimen locked in combat with a Protoceratops, both buried by a collapsing dune.
The Gobi ceratopsian found with nests and eggs, and probably the origin of the griffin legend.
A Mongolian ankylosaurid of the arid Late Cretaceous, with looping nasal passages that may have cooled or moistened the air it breathed.
A ten-metre tyrannosaur of Shandong, from bone beds that also hold the giant duckbill Shantungosaurus.
The largest ornithischian known: a flat-headed duck-bill fifteen metres long from Shandong.
A long-snouted, long-legged hopper twenty centimetres long -- an early eutherian built like an elephant shrew.
The oldest gilled mushroom known, in 99-million-year-old Burmese amber and already entirely modern in form.
The therapsids with a secondary palate, differentiated teeth and probably fur: the line that produces mammals in the Late Triassic.
Small mammal-like cynodonts, herbivorous survivors of the synapsid line into the dinosaur age.
A parrot-beaked early ceratopsian, the most abundant dinosaur of the Jehol beds.
Bennettitales look like cycads and are not; their bisexual cones long confused the search for the origin of flowers.
taxa.hb: stout trunk with a crown of pinnate leaves and flower-like cones

taxa.note: A crested, toothed fishing pterosaur from Brazil's Santana Formation, known from beautifully preserved three-dimensional skulls that reveal the shape of its bony head crest.
A four-metre megaraptoran with large hand claws, from the Early Cretaceous of Japan.
A large ornithopod with a thumb spike, and one of the first dinosaurs recognised as such.
An early beaked bird known from thousands of specimens, many with long ornamental tail streamers.
A badger-sized Jehol mammal found with a juvenile dinosaur in its stomach -- Mesozoic mammals were not all prey.
The Yixian and Jiufotang beds of Liaoning: volcanic ash falls that buried a whole forest ecosystem intact, feathers, stomach contents, colour-bearing melanosomes and all.
An aquatic Jehol plant that is among the earliest fossils confidently identified as a flowering plant.
taxa.hb: aquatic herb

taxa.note: The first dinosaur found with unambiguous filamentous feathers, and later with its ginger-and-white banded tail decoded.
A spinosaurid known from its conical, fluted fish-catching teeth, from the Early Cretaceous rivers of Thailand.
A twenty-metre titanosaur-line sauropod of the Early Cretaceous of north-east Thailand.
A four-to-five-metre armoured dinosaur with spikes along its flanks and a solid shield of fused armour over its hips.
A small bony-tongued fish that filled the Jehol lakes by the million -- the commonest vertebrate fossil of the Early Cretaceous of north-east Asia.
A fish-eating theropod from the English Wealden with a crocodile snout and a thirty-centimetre thumb claw; fish scales were found in its stomach.
A broad-snouted crocodyliform of Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous swamps -- among the first to look and live like the alligators of today.
The whip-tailed sauropods -- Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Supersaurus: twenty-five metres and more of neck and tail on a comparatively light body.
A Chinese sauropod with a neck half its total length -- among the longest necks any animal has had.
A slender sphenodontian of the Solnhofen lagoon shores -- a cousin of the living tuatara, whose group was then one of the most varied among small reptiles.
A stegosaur up to eight metres long with paired spikes rather than broad plates along its back -- the commonest stegosaur of Late Jurassic Europe.
The Solnhofen 'first bird', a feathered dinosaur on a Bavarian lagoon at Laurasia's Tethyan edge.
taxa.hb: arboreal or short-flight glider

taxa.note: A long-tailed pterosaur of the same lagoons, some specimens preserving the wing membrane and throat pouch.
One of the oldest true salamanders, twenty centimetres long, from the lake beds of the Late Jurassic of Kazakhstan.
The apex predator of Jurassic Sichuan, ten metres long, hunting Mamenchisaurus and the local stegosaurs.
A small pterosaur whose fossils first showed that pterosaurs were furred: its body was covered in hair-like fibres.
A toothless ceratosaur whose young had teeth and lost them as they grew into beaked plant-eaters -- a change no other dinosaur is known to have made.
An early crested tyrannosauroid from the Jurassic of Xinjiang, small and long-armed, 90 million years before T. rex.
A seven-metre stegosaur of the Late Jurassic of Sichuan with pointed plates in pairs along its back.
A beaver-tailed, swimming mammaliaform with preserved fur -- evidence Jurassic mammals were not all generic shrews.
A cat-sized heterodontosaurid with long bristle-like filaments along its back and tail.
A seven-to-eight-metre metriacanthosaurid; bite wounds on its skull show that big theropods fought one another face to face.
A shrew-sized climber of the Late Jurassic claimed as the oldest eutherian -- the line leading to placental mammals -- though its age and its place in the tree are debated.
A pterosaur that combined the long tail of the early kind with the head and neck of the later -- a 'modular' intermediate; one was preserved with an egg.
A frog-mouthed anurognathid pterosaur covered in fuzz, which hawked insects at dusk in the Jurassic forests of northern China.
A five-metre theropod with a single hollow crest running from its nose to behind its eyes, from the Junggar Basin, then a well-watered lowland.
One of the earliest stegosaurs, from Middle Jurassic Sichuan, still with teeth at the front of its jaws.
A stegosaur of the Middle Jurassic of England and France with tall spines on its shoulders and tail.
A metre-and-a-half plant-eater from Transbaikalia whose body was covered in filaments and whose legs had scales -- a sign that feather-like fuzz was widespread among dinosaurs.
A tritylodontid -- a plant-eating near-mammal -- among the last of its line, from the Bathonian of England and Scotland.
A three-metre, nose-crested early tyrannosauroid from the Bathonian of England, near the root of the tyrannosaur line.
A tiny Middle Jurassic mammal known from jaws found at Stonesfield in Oxfordshire -- among the first Mesozoic mammals ever recognised.
A ten-metre sauropod with a spiked bony club on the end of its tail -- one of the commonest dinosaurs of the Middle Jurassic of Sichuan.
A large Triassic and Jurassic horsetail, successor to the Calamites of the Carboniferous swamps.
The first dinosaur ever formally named, from Oxfordshire, decades before anyone had the concept of a dinosaur.
One of the earliest water-dwelling turtles, from the Middle Jurassic lagoons of the Isle of Skye -- evidence that turtles took to the water early.
A small early tyrannosauroid from the Middle Jurassic of Siberia, a proceratosaurid like Guanlong.
A four-metre tetanuran of the Middle Jurassic of Sichuan, named for the gas company whose digging found it.
Crocodile-shaped amphibians, from newt-sized to five metres, that ruled rivers and swamps for 200 million years before crocodiles took the job.
Spiders. Silk first for lining burrows; aerial webs came once there were flying insects worth catching.
Frogs. The jumping body plan was in place by the Early Jurassic and has hardly changed.
A long-tailed pterosaur of the Toarcian with a one-metre wingspan and interlocking fangs at the tip of its jaws for seizing fish.
A seven-metre sauropodomorph of the Lufeng beds with self-sharpening, spoon-shaped teeth like a sauropod's.
Mid-sized early sauropodomorphs of Early Jurassic Gondwana and beyond; nests of Massospondylus eggs show the young hatched toothless and helpless.
A hybodont shark with a spine before each dorsal fin and two kinds of teeth, for fish and for shellfish; the commonest shark of Mesozoic seas and rivers.
An early armoured dinosaur, at the base of the lineage leading to stegosaurs and ankylosaurs.
A rabbit-sized tritylodontid, a gnawing plant-eater among the last of the non-mammal cynodonts.
A five-metre crested theropod of the Lufeng beds, the Asian cousin of Dilophosaurus.
A two-gram mammaliaform with a large brain for its size and the ear bones separated from the jaw, as in true mammals.
The common early sauropodomorph of Yunnan, six to nine metres long; embryos in its eggs preserve some of the oldest known organic remains in a dinosaur.
A big-headed early pterosaur with a 1.4-metre wingspan and two kinds of teeth; its legs and claws suggest it climbed well and hunted on the ground as much as in the air.
A dipterid fern whose large leaves spread like the fingers of a hand, meshed with a fine grid of veins -- a hallmark of the humid Late Triassic and Early Jurassic in both hemispheres.
A tiny insect-eater known from teeth washed into cave fissures on limestone islands of the Early Jurassic sea; its triangle of cusps is an early step toward the teeth of all later mammals.
Deep-bodied, armour-scaled fishes that split into species flocks in the rift lakes that opened as Pangaea began to break apart -- as cichlids have in the African lakes today.
Conifers spreading through the dry Triassic interior: the first forests built by plants that could survive a real dry season.
Beaked, tusked herbivorous therapsids that become the most abundant large land animals on Earth.
A horsetail with paired leaves fused into sheaths, common through the Permian and Triassic of Gondwana.
Giant Triassic relatives of grasshoppers with wings spanning up to 36 centimetres and grasping forelegs; patches on their wings may have flashed or rattled like a cicada's.
Long-necked, bipedal plant-eaters up to ten metres: the first dinosaurs to grow large, found in herds in Late Triassic Europe.

Peltasperm seed ferns with pimpled leaves and seeds carried under umbrella-like discs. One of the few plant lines to ride through the end-Permian extinction, they mark the earliest Triassic and again the Rhaetian, just before the end-Triassic extinction took them.
An early long-necked sauropodomorph, and among the first genuinely large herbivorous dinosaurs.
An early pterosaur with a complex tooth battery, already fully capable of powered flight.
A flat, broad-headed plagiosaurid amphibian that lay on lake beds like a flatfish, gulping prey that swam over it; it kept external gills all its life.
A reptile whose neck is longer than the rest of it combined, with only twelve vertebrae in it.
A slender-snouted phytosaur of the Late Triassic Tethys coasts; some lie in marine limestones, so it may have fished at sea as well as in rivers.
An elephant-sized dicynodont of the latest Triassic -- perhaps nine tonnes, walking erect -- the last and largest of a line that had been on land since the Permian.

A dipterid fern with a fan of broad, net-veined leaflets. Its only living relatives are the umbrella ferns of South-East Asian clearings; in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic the family was one of the commonest on Earth.
A flat-skulled giant amphibian that packed drying Late Triassic lakes across Europe by the hundreds, the type genus for the metoposaurid family.
A giant Triassic horsetail with stems up to ten centimetres thick and several metres tall -- the scouring rush scaled up, standing in reed beds along the river plains.
A small aetosaur, a metre to a metre and a half long, armoured in rows of plates; one slab holds 24 juveniles buried together.
A ginkgophyte with long, tongue-shaped leaves instead of fans -- one of several experiments in the Ginkgo line that did not outlast the Triassic.
A three-metre aetosaur: an armoured, pig-snouted plant-eater of the crocodile line, rooting in the soil of Late Triassic river plains.

A pig-sized rhynchosaur with a hooked beak and grinding plates of teeth. In the Carnian it was so common that it makes up most of the fossils in the same beds in Scotland, India, Brazil and Argentina.
A slim, two-metre dinosaur cousin with a beak-tipped jaw; droppings attributed to it are full of small beetles, so it ate insects as well as plants.
A conifer of Triassic river plains, part of the flora that recolonised the land after the end-Permian coal gap.
Flat-headed giant amphibians that mass-died in drying Triassic lakes across Laurasia.
A peltasperm seed fern with long, leathery, deeply toothed leaves -- the characteristic plant of Middle and Late Triassic floras from the Alps to Central Asia and the Urals.
A three-metre capitosaur whose ear notch closed into a ring -- a top predator of Late Triassic lakes and rivers from Europe to Greenland and Thailand.
Plant-eating cynodonts with broad grinding cheek teeth -- the commonest herbivores of many Gondwanan Triassic faunas.
A long-necked, semi-aquatic fish-catcher representing an early stage of the sauropterygian move into the sea.
One of the largest amphibians that ever lived: a six-metre, flat-headed temnospondyl of Middle Triassic lakes, with fangs that poked up through holes in the top of its snout.
The ammonite that dates the German Muschelkalk so precisely its zones are named after it.
The big tusked dicynodonts of the Triassic -- ox-sized, beaked herbivores found on every part of Pangaea.
A tall fern of the red Buntsandstein plains -- among the first plants to re-vegetate a landscape that the end-Permian extinction had stripped bare.
A metre-tall unbranched lycopod that stands in for an entire vanished forest flora.
taxa.hb: unbranched, in disturbed coastal ground

taxa.note: A pike-shaped ray-finned fish with a long toothed snout, an ambush predator of Triassic seas and lakes worldwide.
Crocodile-line archosaurs that walked upright on pillar legs: the top land predators of the Triassic, before dinosaurs had the role.
Pig-sized reptiles with a parrot beak and shearing tooth plates. In places they are half of all the fossils found -- then gone by the Norian.
A pig-sized dicynodont that survives the extinction and then makes up most of the land vertebrate fauna of the entire planet.
taxa.hb: burrowing herbivore

taxa.note: An early archosaur, sprawling and crocodile-like, at the root of the lineage that will produce dinosaurs and birds.
Kangaroos radiate as grasslands spread across the drying interior.
Queen Alexandra's birdwing, the largest butterfly, with a wingspan of 28 cm.
The koala, living on eucalypt leaves too poor and too toxic for almost anything else.
The Tasmanian devil, largest surviving marsupial carnivore; on the mainland until about 3,000 years ago.
Spinifex: needle-leaved hummock grasses covering a quarter of Australia, and shelter for most of its desert reptiles.
A three-tonne wombat relative, the largest marsupial ever, gone from Australia around 46,000 years ago.
The marsupial lion, a powerful ambush predator with the strongest bite of any known mammal for its size.
A short-faced giant kangaroo browsing shrubs on one-toed feet.
A seven-metre monitor lizard, Australia's largest terrestrial predator until the megafauna extinction.
Early marsupial 'lions' with bolt-cutter premolars appear in the Miocene rainforest fauna.
Mihirungs or 'thunder birds': flightless giant fowl to 600 kg, relatives of ducks rather than emus.
Australasia's own crocodiles, some of them land-going and some reaching Fiji and New Caledonia; the last died out after people arrived.
The Chinchilla Local Fauna of the Darling Downs, Queensland -- a Pliocene assemblage recording Australia's rainforest-to-woodland shift, misfiled by name-collision with the South American rodent.
Banksias of the kwongan heath, one of the world's richest floras on the poorest soil.
The thorny devil: an ant-eating lizard whose skin channels dew to its mouth.
Koalas, once several genera in Miocene rainforest; one species remains, specialised on eucalypt leaves.
A sheep-sized tree-dwelling marsupial herbivore, mass-preserved in Riversleigh cave pools.
An early koala of the Miocene rainforests, smaller than today's and with a less specialised diet.
A Riversleigh platypus that, unlike the living one, kept functional teeth as an adult.
A small early kangaroo that probably bounded on all fours rather than hopping on two feet.
A 'killer kangaroo': a rat-kangaroo relative with serrated slicing premolars, probably an omnivore that took small animals.
Penguins, flightless divers since the Paleocene; several Eocene and Oligocene species stood as tall as a person.
The emperor penguin, the only bird that breeds through the Antarctic winter.
A flightless midge, the largest wholly terrestrial animal on the continent.
The entire Antarctic land fauna above the microscopic -- a few dozen species surviving in moss and under stones.
The crabeater seal, the most numerous large mammal on Earth after us, sieving krill through lobed teeth on the Antarctic pack ice.
Antarctic hairgrass, one of just two flowering plants on the continent.
Antarctic pearlwort, one of only two flowering plants native to Antarctica.
A green alga that thrives on the guano-soaked ground of penguin rookeries, the most conspicuous plant life on the Antarctic coast.
True seals, which arose in the North Atlantic and reached the Antarctic pack ice by the late Miocene.
A bushy beard lichen, among the largest land organisms of the Antarctic Peninsula.
Oribatid mites, the slow armoured grazers of leaf litter and moss, in the soil of every land ecosystem since the Devonian.
Weevils of southern South America whose fossils lie in the Meyer Desert beds, 500 km from the Pole: tundra insects that outlasted the first ice sheets.
A fungus farming algae or cyanobacteria inside itself. Among the first things to colonise bare rock, and still the pioneer on newly exposed ground.
A small marsupial from Seymour Island: proof that mammals crossed from South America to Australia through a forested Antarctica.
Endemic hoofed mammals, some convergent on horses and camels, unique to South America.
Moths from the Jurassic, butterflies from the Cretaceous: scaled wings and, once flowers existed, a coiled tongue to reach nectar.
Ants. Rare in Cretaceous amber, then from the Eocene on the dominant small predators and soil-movers of nearly every land habitat.
Beetles. From the Permian on, the most species-rich order of animals there has ever been.
Grasshoppers, crickets and katydids: the singing insects, and the great grazers of the insect world.
A small ornithopod of the high-latitude Cretaceous forests of the Antarctic Peninsula.
An Antarctic fossil placing modern bird lineages -- specifically waterfowl relatives -- before the extinction.
The first ankylosaur from Antarctica, from the James Ross Basin of the still-forested Cretaceous continent.
The big beaked plant-eaters with grinding tooth batteries, from Camptosaurus to the duck-bills -- the commonest large herbivores of the Cretaceous.
The flying reptiles: wings of skin stretched on one enormously long finger, from sparrow-sized to the span of a small aircraft.
Cypresses, junipers, redwoods and their kin; their fossil wood lies in the Miocene lavas of Kerguelen, now a treeless island.
Giant toothless pterosaurs with stiff necks as long as a giraffe's, stalking prey on the ground like storks.
The 'opposite birds': toothed, clawed-winged fliers that were the commonest birds of the Cretaceous and left no descendants.
The Asian elephant lineage, which arose in Africa about five million years ago and spread across southern Asia.
The Indian peafowl.
Grey langurs, leaf-eating monkeys from Sri Lanka to 4,000 m in the Himalaya.
The nilgai or blue bull, the largest Asian antelope.
Dipterocarps, which dominate South-East Asian rainforest to a degree no family manages anywhere else, and mast-fruit across whole regions at once.
Sal, the dipterocarp that forms the forests of the Himalayan foothills and central India.
The common reed, walling lake margins and deltas on every continent but Antarctica.
The largest ape that ever lived, a three-metre orangutan relative known almost entirely from teeth found in Chinese caves and apothecary shops.
The tiger, from Siberian taiga to Sumatran rainforest.
A large proboscidean with tusks set so close together that the trunk hung to one side; its dwarfed island forms reached Flores and Timor.
The banyan, a strangler fig that spreads on aerial roots until one tree is a grove.
Salt-excreting shrubs holding the fringes of oases and wadis.
Tropical pitcher plants; the largest hold litres and have caught rats.
The gorilla-like chalicothere of Miocene Eurasia, walking on its knuckles to keep its hooked claws sharp.
Cats arose in Eurasia, reached North America about 18 Ma and South America with the interchange. Ambush predators built around a killing bite.
Rhinoceroses were once the commonest large herbivores of the northern continents, with hornless, hippo-like and woolly forms; five species remain.
Lemur-like early primates that spread through the greenhouse forests of the Eocene right up to the Arctic.
The 'walking whale' of Indo-Pakistani Eocene coasts, a crocodile-like stage in whale origins.
A raccoon-sized, chevrotain-like artiodactyl with thick, dense leg bones for wading -- the closest known relative of whales.
The earliest whale: a wolf-sized, four-legged land animal of the Eocene of Pakistan, with the ear bones that mark every whale since.
Fifty-million-year-old amber from Gujarat holds a dipterocarp rainforest, and insects with Asian relatives: India was already trading life across a narrowing sea.
A Vastan lignite mammal near the root of odd-toed ungulates, recording India's brief faunal isolation.
Termites: social cockroaches that digest wood with the microbes in their gut, and recycle most of a tropical forest's dead timber.
Dragonflies, damselflies and their giant Palaeozoic cousins the griffinflies: aerial predators for 325 million years.
A horned abelisaur theropod from the Lameta beds, hunting amid the erupting Deccan Traps.
A titanosaur of latest-Cretaceous India whose nesting grounds are preserved as fossil egg clutches.
A 3.5 m snake fossilised coiled around a titanosaur egg in a nest, waiting for the hatchling.
Baleen whales reach modern size as intensified coastal upwelling concentrates their food into dense patches.
The California sea lion, breeding on the desert islands of the Gulf of California and the Pacific coast.
The Humboldt or jumbo squid, hunting in shoals of thousands along the eastern Pacific.
The totoaba, a two-metre drum found only in the Gulf of California, spawning at the Colorado River's mouth.
A calcified green alga that breaks down into carbonate sand -- much of a tropical beach is dead Halimeda.
Flowering plants that returned to the sea in the Cretaceous, binding shallow sediment and nursing juvenile fish and turtles.
Sargassum weeds, attached on warm rocky shores and, in two Atlantic species, drifting free in mid-ocean.

Dasyclad green algae, single cells the size of a finger with whorls of branches, calcified enough to be rock-formers in Palaeozoic and Mesozoic shelf limestones; a few, like the mermaid's wineglass, survive.
Microscopic plated algae that take over the open ocean and start building chalk.
The vaquita, the smallest and rarest cetacean, confined to the turbid head of the Gulf of California.
Pseudo-toothed birds: seabirds with bony spikes along the beak and wingspans to six metres, gliding the oceans from the Palaeocene to the Pliocene.
The giant squid, reaching twelve metres and known for most of history only from carcasses and sperm-whale scars.
The living Nautilus, a survivor of the once-vast shelled-cephalopod dynasties, still haunts these depths.
A macropredatory shark perhaps sixteen metres long, known almost entirely from its teeth.
taxa.hb: pelagic macropredator

taxa.note: A marine ground sloth that grazed seagrass off the Peruvian coast -- a lineage no one predicted.
The coelacanth, a living lobe-finned fish, survives in deep refugia off the Comoros.
An early pinniped, at the transition of carnivorans into fully marine life.
Coralline red algae, crusts as hard as the rock they grow on, cementing reef rubble into reef; on a modern reef they hold more of the framework together than the corals do.
Manta and devil rays, filter-feeders that leap clear of the water in schools of thousands.
Hard-shelled sea turtles: green, hawksbill, loggerhead and their Cretaceous forerunners.
Sixgill sharks, a lineage little changed since the Jurassic, cruising the dark continental slopes.
Bone-eating worms that bore into whale skeletons on the sea floor; their traces go back to plesiosaur bones.
Krill: swarming shrimp-like crustaceans. In the Southern Ocean they are the single link between diatoms and everything larger -- whales, seals, penguins and fish all feed on them.
Flying fishes, gliding tens of metres on enlarged fins to escape tuna and dolphinfish.
The early whales, from four-legged waders to the fully marine, serpent-bodied Basilosaurus of warm Eocene seas.
A thick-shelled clam of Seymour Island, in the Antarctic shelf sands from the last Cretaceous stage through the Eocene, before the ice.
Grenadiers or rattails, the commonest fishes of the continental slope and the abyssal plain.
Single-celled algae in glass shells. From the Oligocene on their blooms feed the cold oceans and their remains pile up as diatomite.
The megatooth sharks, a lineage of giant whale-hunting predators running from the Eocene to Otodus megalodon.
A tall-spired horn snail of warm shallow water, in vast numbers in the brackish Sarmatian sea of the Paratethys.
The 'saber-toothed herring', a fanged predatory fish found in Late Cretaceous seas world-wide.
Big flat clams littering Cretaceous seafloors, sometimes shells over a metre across.
A straight-shelled ammonite so abundant it zones the entire seaway; the chalk records its coccolith plankton.
A thick, coiled oyster with a spiral beak, cemented to the Cretaceous sea floor in beds you can walk on in Texas and Alabama.
A winged trigoniid clam of Cretaceous shores, common in Japan and the American Gulf Coast.
Keeled planktonic foraminifera raining onto the Cretaceous ocean floor.
They displace corals as the main tropical reef builder for much of the Cretaceous, and die at the K-Pg.
The heart urchin of the English chalk, whose changing shape up through the cliffs was one of the first fossil lineages read as evolution.
A large disc-shaped ammonite, some shells punctured by mosasaur tooth-marks.
Large conical foraminifera of Cretaceous carbonate platforms, big enough to see without a lens.
A large, heavily ribbed trigoniid clam, the shell that paves the Early Cretaceous shores of Argentina, and known too from Japan and South Africa.
A chimaera of the Eromanga sea, known from its tooth plates in the opal fields of South Australia.
A ribbed, unequal-valved scallop of Cretaceous shelves, one of the commonest bivalves of the chalk seas.
A slit-shelled sea snail of Jurassic and Cretaceous shelves; its relatives survive today only in deep water.
A heart urchin of Early Cretaceous shelf marls, the ancestor of Micraster's line, burrowing in the Tethyan mud.
A giant open-coiled Aptian ammonite, over a metre across in the Eromanga sea of Australia, whose shell was a slow spiral of separate whorls.
A small plesiosaur of the cold Eromanga sea, found in the opal mines of Coober Pedy with crests on its skull.
A burrowing lobster of Jurassic and Cretaceous sea floors, whose Thalassinoides-type burrows outnumber its bodies by millions.
The ammonite that defines the base of the Aptian, in the seas that widened as the Atlantic opened south.
An open-coiled ammonite, whorls not touching, ribbed and spined, of the Hauterivian seas of the Tethys and Neuquen.
A globular, strongly ribbed ammonite of the Valanginian, known from Europe to Argentina, Mexico and South Africa.
The smallest and most numerous photosynthesiser known, making a large share of the oxygen produced by the open ocean.
Tiny vase-shaped plankton that zone the Tethyan latest-Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.
A ribbed Valanginian ammonite of the Tethys and the young Atlantic, the standard fossil of the Neocomian.
A calcified red alga growing in nodules and crusts on Ordovician to Cretaceous reefs; sliced, its pink and grey banding is the 'beetroot stone' of Jurassic England.
A metriorhynchid sea crocodile with a deep, short skull and serrated teeth -- a macropredator that fed on marine reptiles, the killer whale of its seas.
A thick, ornamented triangular clam that burrowed Jurassic and Cretaceous sands worldwide; a lone survivor, Neotrigonia, still lives off Australia.
Tangled tubes of a calcified cyanobacterium, coating shells and grains into oncoids on Cambrian to Jurassic sea floors: the commonest microbial fossil of the Palaeozoic shelf.
The largest ray-finned fish that has ever lived, sixteen metres of filter-feeder from the Oxford Clay, straining the Jurassic sea like a whale shark.
An ichthyosaur with eyes the size of dinner plates, the largest of any vertebrate relative to its body, for hunting squid in the dark.
The rorquals -- blue, fin, minke and humpback's kin -- lunge-feeders on krill and shoaling fish since the late Miocene.
The orca, the ocean's top predator, hunting from the pack ice to the tropics in family pods that pass their hunting techniques down the generations.
The humpback whale, with flippers a third of its length, migrating between polar feeding grounds and tropical calving waters.
Free-floating sargassum, the golden weed of the Sargasso Sea, carrying its own community of fish, crabs and turtles.
Turtle grass, forming the great seagrass meadows of the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico.
Pyrosomes: glowing colonial tunicates, hollow tubes that can grow longer than a whale.
A cold-water scallop of the Antarctic shelf since the Miocene; its relative Adamussium colbecki grows under the sea ice today.
Tunas: warm-blooded, ocean-crossing predators built for sustained speed.
The vampire squid, last of an order older than the dinosaurs, drifting in the oxygen-minimum zone on marine snow.
Sperm whales in their Miocene variety, from dwarf forms to Livyatan, a raptorial hunter of other whales.
A venus clam of the cold southern shelves, in Antarctic sediments from the Palaeocene onward and on Patagonian shores today.
Mako sharks, the fastest of all sharks and ocean-wide hunters of tuna and swordfish.
Giant marine lizards, relatives of monitors and snakes, that took the top-predator role in every Late Cretaceous sea.
The crow shark, a scavenger of the Cretaceous seas whose serrated teeth are found lodged in dinosaur bones washed out to sea.
A hook-shaped scaphitid ammonite of the Pierre Shale and the Maastrichtian chalk, one of the very last ammonites before the impact.
A metre-long sea turtle of the Niobrara chalk, close to the stem of the living sea turtles.
A plesiosaur with seventy-two neck vertebrae and a neck seven metres long, from the Kansas chalk; its first describer put the head on the tail.
A three-metre sea turtle of the Western Interior Seaway, ancestor in form to Archelon, with a shell reduced to struts.
A deep-bodied plethodid fish of the Niobrara sea with a fan-like dorsal fin the length of its back.
The 'Ginsu shark', seven metres long, whose bite marks are on the bones of mosasaurs and plesiosaurs from Kansas to Europe.
A shark with pavement teeth for crushing clams, ten metres long, a Cretaceous durophage whose teeth litter the chalk seas of two hemispheres.
A sharp-keeled Albian ammonite of the Gulf Coast, Peru, Venezuela and Africa: the fauna of a tropical Atlantic that had just been made.
A knobbed, thick-ribbed Albian ammonite found on every continent, in the Western Interior Seaway and the Tethys alike.
Sediment bound by microbial mats. They come back in force after every mass extinction, when the grazers that normally crop them are gone.
A Boreal Valanginian ammonite of the northern seas, from England to Siberia and Canada, marking the province the Tethyan forms did not reach.
Coiled cephalopods diversifying fast; they will become the single best index fossil of the Mesozoic.
A tuna-shaped pachycormid fish of the Jurassic sea, a fast predator of the same family as the giant filter-feeder Leedsichthys.
A wing-shelled bivalve of lagoons and shallow shelves, in the Permian, Triassic and Jurassic of every continent.
A horseshoe crab preserved at the end of its own death-track across the anoxic mud.
A thick-shelled bivalve of Cretaceous shelf muds, some species reaching a metre across, and often the only large fossil in an otherwise barren chalk.
A large evolute ammonite with forked ribs, common enough in the Oxfordian to be found in Europe, East Africa, Cuba and Japan.
A long-necked plesiosaur of the Oxford Clay with a hundred needle teeth, netting small fish and squid.
A crocodile rebuilt for the open sea: flippers, a tail fin, no armour, hunting fish and ammonites in the Oxford Clay.
A short-necked pliosaur with a skull well over a metre long, hunting other marine reptiles.
taxa.hb: pelagic pursuit predator

taxa.note: Stone corals appear from nowhere and rebuild the reef ecosystem the Permian destroyed; every modern reef descends from them.
A cold-water coral building reefs in the dark, hundreds of metres down, along continental slopes and seamounts.
A small seagrass of the Red Sea and western Indian Ocean, growing from the shallows to fifty metres down.
Giant kelp; kelp forests establish as a new nearshore biome in newly cool coastal waters.
The seagrass of Saya de Malha, a drowned bank in mid-ocean carrying the largest seagrass meadow on Earth.
'Sea sawdust', a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium whose rust-coloured blooms streak warm, nutrient-poor seas.
The sperm whale, the largest toothed predator alive, diving past two kilometres to hunt squid in the dark.
Star-shaped calcareous nannoplankton whose extinction near 1.9 million years ago is used to close out the warm Pliocene ocean.
Large brown algae forming underwater forests on cool rocky coasts. A Neogene novelty, and the habitat sea otters and abalone depend on.
A terebratulid brachiopod of New Zealand's shelves, where lamp-shells are still abundant in the cool south.
Planktic foraminifera colonise the open water column, becoming a permanent part of the ocean's carbon cycle.
The geoduck, a deep-burrowing clam with a siphon longer than its shell, in cool shelf sands from the Cretaceous to the present; the commonest fossil shell of Antarctica's Miocene.
Trough shells, burrowing clams of sandy shores; the Paratethys of the late Miocene was so full of them that its beds are called the Mactra limestones.
A jointed, bushy bryozoan of cool shelf seas; in the Southern Ocean bryozoans build the sea-floor thickets that a reef's corals build in the tropics.
A small, hairy-shelled clam of cool and deep water, one of the commonest bivalves of the Antarctic and subantarctic shelves.
Squid-like cephalopods whose bullet-shaped guards are among the commonest Jurassic fossils.
A late ammonite that grew shells a metre across, among the last of its kind, in the seas of the final Cretaceous stages worldwide.
A ferocious bony fish, sometimes fossilised with an entire swallowed fish inside it.
A planktonic foraminifer with a double keel, the zone fossil of the Late Cretaceous ocean; the K-Pg boundary clay is full of its broken shells.
Layered mounds built by microbial mats trapping and binding sediment: the dominant reef of the first three billion years, and often the only fossil a Precambrian shelf preserves.
A giant short-necked pliosaur, apex predator of the cold Cretaceous sea over central Australia.
The Antarctic toothfish, a two-metre notothenioid with antifreeze in its blood, top fish predator under the Ross Sea ice.
Antarctic krill: swarms of hundreds of millions of tonnes on which the whole Southern Ocean food web rests.
The Antarctic silverfish, the herring of the Southern Ocean, the link between the krill and the penguins, seals and whales.
A rhynchonellid brachiopod of New Zealand and the Southern Ocean, a lamp-shell lineage still common where the water is cold.
The bowhead whale, adapted to break sea ice, is the signature large animal of the modern Arctic.
The narwhal, whose spiral tusk is a single tooth carrying millions of nerve endings.
Polar cod: it lives in and under the sea ice and is the link between Arctic plankton and everything larger.
The walrus, raking clams from the Arctic shelf and hauling out on ice with its tusks.
Diatoms growing in brine channels within the ice itself, which bloom months before the open water does and start the polar year.
The sea butterfly, a swimming snail a few millimetres across that feeds Arctic cod and whales, and whose thin shell dissolves first as the ocean acidifies.
Clams, mussels, oysters and scallops. They take over the shallow sea floor from brachiopods after the end-Permian and never give it back.
The capelin, the small silver fish that cod, whales and seabirds of the North Atlantic and Arctic all depend on.
Larger benthic forams diversify and become key shelf-carbonate contributors.
The sea angel, a shell-less swimming snail of the polar oceans that hunts sea butterflies with hooked tentacles.
Oceanic dolphins, from spinners to orcas; a late-Miocene radiation that now fills every sea.
A grenadier of the continental slope, its otoliths in New Zealand's Miocene mudstones by the hundred.
A lanternfish genus of a hundred living species, whose otoliths are the commonest fish fossils of Neogene deep-water sediments from New Zealand to Italy.
Lanternfishes, perhaps the most abundant vertebrates on Earth, rising hundreds of metres to the surface every night.
After the Messinian salinity crisis dried the basin, salt-tolerant survivors and Atlantic recolonisers rebuild the fauna.
The great white shark, descended from broad-toothed makos about six million years ago.
The leatherback, a half-tonne turtle that follows jellyfish from the tropics to subpolar water.
Neptune grass: a flowering plant whose meadows anchor the Mediterranean's endemic shelf ecosystem; single clones are thought to be tens of thousands of years old.
Eelgrass, the seagrass of cool northern shores, nursery to cod, scallops and brent geese.
A brackish ostracod that boomed as the Mediterranean's chemistry swung wildly during the salinity crisis.
The cockle, a shallow-burrowing clam of estuaries and brackish lagoons; the Paratethys's low salinity suited it, and its species there ran riot.
Coin-sized benthic foraminifera beginning the bank-building that will define Tethyan shelf carbonates.
taxa.hb: benthic on warm carbonate shelves

taxa.note: The brackish Sarmatian sea of the Paratethys: no corals, no sea urchins, no ammonite kin, but cockles, trough shells and horn snails in beds a hundred metres thick.
The snow leopard, hunting blue sheep across cliff and scree.
The Himalayan griffon, soaring the highest of any vulture.
The bharal, the snow leopard's principal prey.
Beavers. Most fossil ones were burrowers, not dam-builders; the Ice Age giant beaver was the size of a black bear.
The great apes. In the Miocene they ranged from Spain to China; the cooling and drying of Eurasia left them in African and South-East Asian forest.
Deer, the antlered ruminants of the northern forests. They reached South America with the interchange and never got south of the Sahara.
A 'shovel-tusker': a gomphothere whose lower jaw ends in a broad pair of flat tusks, used for stripping bark and cutting plants.
Horses: fifty million years of North American evolution, from four-toed forest browsers to one-toed grazers, exported to the Old World in pulses and then lost at home.
The Andean condor, riding ridge updraughts on a three-metre wingspan.
The vicuna, grazing the altiplano on the finest wool of any mammal.
Aquatic water frogs breathing through skin folds in cold high-altitude lakes.
The spectacled bear of the Andean cloud forest, last of the short-faced bears.
The southern pudu, the world's smallest deer, in the bamboo thickets of the Valdivian forest.
Andean pupfish: a species flock of the high-altitude lakes, centred on Titicaca.
The tropical giant ground sloth, as big as Megatherium, ranging from Brazil through Panama to Florida.
Over 250 species of small lizards from Patagonia to the high Andes -- one of the largest lizard radiations anywhere.
A sheep-sized notoungulate -- one of South America's native hoofed mammals, which evolved in isolation for sixty million years.
The grizzly, ranging from valley floor to alpine tundra.
The mountain goat, on cliffs no predator can follow.
The North American beaver, whose dams engineered the continent's stream valleys.
Black spruce, the tree of cold, wet North American muskeg, able to root into sphagnum.
The American pika, haying all summer on talus slopes and retreating uphill as the mountains warm.
The bald eagle, a fish eagle of North American lakes, rivers and coasts.
The sabre-toothed cat, moving south into a South America that had never seen anything like it.
White-tailed and mule deer, the New World's own deer and its commonest large mammals.
Camels are a North American family. They crossed to Asia about 7 Ma and to South America about 3 Ma, then died out where they began.
Tapirs have barely changed since the Eocene. Today's odd range -- tropical America and Malaya -- is what is left of a family once spread across the north.
A leopard-sized nimravid 'false sabre-tooth', with a bony flange on its jaw to guard its long canines.
A cow-sized entelodont, a 'hell pig' of the Oligocene plains; bite marks show it stored the carcasses of early camels to eat later.
A long-legged 'running rhinoceros', pony-sized and hornless, built for speed on the open Oligocene plains.
The Alpine ibex, grazing near-vertical rock.
The Alpine marmot, hibernating eight months of the year.
The bearded vulture or lammergeier, which lives on bones and drops them on rocks to break them.
Edelweiss, felted white against ultraviolet light on Alpine limestone.
Reindeer lichen, the tundra's dominant winter forage.
The Eurasian lynx, ambush hunter of roe deer in forest and mountain.
The wolverine: a mustelid that kills prey many times its size and caches it in the frozen ground.
The Barbary macaque of the Atlas cedar forests, the only monkey north of the Sahara; in the Pleistocene it ranged to England.
The moose: the largest deer, browsing willow and feeding in boreal lakes, its splayed hooves suited to bog and snow.
The Barbary sheep or aoudad of the Saharan massifs and the Atlas.
The Atlas cedar, forming the high forests of Morocco and Algeria.
A Chadian skull around seven million years old, close to the chimpanzee-human split and arguably on our side of it.
Pigs: Old World omnivores whose rapidly evolving teeth are used to date African hominin sites.
A long-jawed early proboscidean of the Fayum swamps, with short tusks above and below -- a step between Moeritherium and the mastodons.
A small hyrax of the Fayum -- from a time when hyraxes, not antelopes, were Africa's main grazers and browsers.
A sauropod holding its neck high above the canopy, weighing perhaps thirty tonnes; the similar Tendaguru animal from Africa is now placed in its own genus, Giraffatitan.
taxa.hb: high browser with forelimbs longer than hindlimbs

taxa.note: The Late Jurassic Morrison Formation - Allosaurus, Stegosaurus, Apatosaurus, Diplodocus - the archetypal dinosaur bonebed.
A small short-tailed pterosaur from Solnhofen, and the first pterosaur ever described.
A dwarf sauropod six metres long, shrunk by life on the islands of the Jurassic European archipelago.
A short-skulled stegosaur of the early Morrison with low, oval back plates; one skeleton preserves the horny sheath that covered a plate.
A small feathered paravian preserved well enough for its actual colour pattern to be reconstructed from melanosomes.
A gliding mammaliaform with a preserved membrane, roughly 100 million years before bats.
An early large sauropod, originally mistaken for a giant marine reptile.
A crested early theropod, six metres long and nothing like its film portrayal.
A shrew-sized nocturnal insectivore with a mammalian jaw joint -- close to the origin of mammals.
A slender early theropod dinosaur, hundreds found together at Ghost Ranch in Pangaea's western deserts.
taxa.hb: gracile bipedal predator, gregarious

taxa.note: Armoured, pig-snouted herbivorous archosaurs common in northern Triassic red beds; extinct at the end-Triassic mass extinction.
A mouse-sized haramiyid of the latest Triassic with many-cusped grinding teeth -- part of the first wave of mammal-like animals.
A slender, long-snouted phytosaur from the Late Triassic of the eastern United States, crocodile-like in build though unrelated, with nostrils set back near the eyes rather than the snout tip.
A broad, flat-backed aetosaur -- a three-metre armoured plant-eater of the crocodile line, common on the Late Triassic floodplains of the American Southwest.
A seven-metre phytosaur, crocodile-shaped but not a crocodile: its nostrils sat on a mound in front of its eyes, not at the tip of its snout.
A stout, beaked reptile two metres long with broad three-cusped cheek teeth -- a Late Triassic plant-eater that looks like a lizard but belongs to the archosaur side of the reptile tree.
A small, short-faced ornithopod of the polar forests of Early Cretaceous Victoria, then well inside the Antarctic Circle.
The last of the giant temnospondyls, five metres long, surviving in the cold rift-valley rivers of polar Australia where crocodiles could not live.
A small ankylosaur, about three metres long, from the Early Cretaceous of Queensland, with extra bony rods along its backbone.
A short-necked sauropod with two rows of tall spines down its neck, perhaps carrying a sail or a display of horn.
A dicraeosaurid with very long, forward-curving spines on its neck -- a defensive palisade, or the frame of a display.
The Late Jurassic Tanzanian beds preserve Giraffatitan and Kentrosaurus - Africa's answer to the Morrison.
Australia's Jurassic sauropod, about fifteen metres long -- one of very few windows on the continent's Jurassic land life.
A fifteen-metre sauropod of the Moroccan High Atlas with unusually long legs for its body -- a brachiosaur-like build reached independently.
A thirteen-metre early sauropod of the Middle Jurassic of Niger, once reconstructed with tail spikes like Shunosaurus's.
True flies -- midges, mosquitoes, hoverflies -- with the hind wings reduced to balancing knobs.
A two-and-a-half-metre temnospondyl of the Early Jurassic -- a late survivor of the big amphibians in the cool rivers of southern Gondwana.
A nine-metre early sauropod of the Toarcian, known from a skeleton preserved almost complete, skull and all.
A five-metre early ceratosaur of the Toarcian High Atlas, near the root of the line that led to the abelisaurids.
A fifteen-metre sauropod of the Early to Middle Jurassic, found with juveniles in a lake-margin community that also held the predator Piatnitzkysaurus.
A four-to-five-metre megalosauroid, one of the southern cousins of Megalosaurus from the Early to Middle Jurassic of Patagonia.
A nine-metre early sauropod from a single Early Jurassic bone bed in India, with the lightly built limbs of a transitional form.
An early sauropodomorph from Mount Kirkpatrick, 4,000 m up in the Transantarctic Mountains.
One of the earliest true sauropods, fourteen metres long, from a single Early Jurassic bone bed in central India holding at least six individuals.
A three-centimetre frog from the Early Jurassic of Patagonia, one of the oldest that looks entirely modern.
One of the earliest true sauropods, from Zimbabwe, as Gondwana begins to break apart.
A crested theropod from the Transantarctic Mountains, showing dinosaurs living at high southern latitudes.
A six-metre predator with a crest running across its skull from side to side, from the Early Jurassic of the Transantarctic Mountains -- dug out at 4,000 metres, 650 km from the South Pole.
An early sauropodomorph from South African Jurassic red beds, known even from embryos in the egg.
A metre-long, lightly built early ornithischian, fast and bipedal, with leaf-shaped teeth; two found curled together suggest it may have slept out the dry seasons in shelter.
A ten-centimetre, shrew-like morganucodontan of the earliest Jurassic -- one of the first near-mammals: nocturnal, insect-eating and probably furred.
A turkey-sized early ornithischian from the Karoo with three kinds of teeth, including tusks, in one jaw.
A metre-long crocodylomorph of the Early Jurassic with long legs for running on land -- the kind of animal all crocodiles descend from.
Slender, hollow-boned early theropods two or three metres long: the first widespread predatory dinosaurs.
The forked-leaf seed fern that defines Gondwanan Triassic forest and marks the end of the coal gap.
taxa.hb: forked-frond tree and shrub

taxa.note: An early podocarp relative with flat needles in two ranks, like a yew's -- evidence that the southern conifer family that still dominates New Zealand and the Andes was already Gondwanan in the Triassic.
The seed-bearing organ of Dicroidium, the seed fern that dominated Triassic Gondwana.
A heavy ten-metre sauropodomorph of Late Triassic Argentina, already walking on all fours.
A two-metre, slender predator among the first dinosaurs of all -- like Herrerasaurus, a hunter from the time when dinosaurs were still a small part of the fauna.
A boar-sized traversodont cynodont, the commonest herbivore of Ischigualasto -- and found in India too, across an unbroken Gondwana.
One of the earliest dinosaurs of all: a three- to six-metre predator from Ischigualasto, when dinosaurs were still a minor part of the fauna.
A seven-metre rauisuchian, the apex predator of Ischigualasto while the first dinosaurs ran about its feet.
A metre-long, light-boned dinosaur from the dawn of the group, with teeth suited to both meat and plants.
A hippo-sized dicynodont that shared its floodplain with the first dinosaurs -- among the last big beaked herbivores of a line that had been on land since the Permian.
Strap-leaved conifer shrubs of the voltzialean line, the commonest plant on many Late Triassic Gondwanan floodplains: thickets of it lined the channels while Dicroidium forest stood behind.
A seven-metre crocodile-line predator with a deep skull, walking erect on pillar legs -- the top carnivore of the Middle to Late Triassic river plains of southern Brazil.
A three-metre, beaked dicynodont, the big plant-eater of the Middle Triassic; a tall crest on its skull anchored the jaw muscles that sheared tough seed-fern leaves.
A two-and-a-half-metre capitosaur of Gondwana's Middle Triassic rivers; a complete skeleton was dug out of a Sydney brick pit.
A dog-sized cynodont with differentiated teeth and probably fur -- most of the way to a mammal.
taxa.hb: terrestrial predator

taxa.note: A 60-centimetre, lightly armoured reptile close to the root of the archosaurs, the group of crocodiles, pterosaurs and dinosaurs. It could probably rise onto its hind legs to run.
A sphenophyte of the Glossopteris swamps with whorls of long, narrow leaves joined at the base into a collar -- the southern counterpart of Calamites.
A long-necked carnivore two to three metres long, one of the earliest members of the bird line of archosaurs -- still walking on all fours, with a crocodile-like ankle, before dinosaurs existed.
A five-metre, big-headed archosauriform, the heaviest land predator of the early Middle Triassic -- a sign of how fast large hunters came back after the end-Permian extinction.

A cat-sized cynodont of the earliest Triassic that lived in burrows -- one was found curled up in its tunnel beside an injured amphibian. Its ribs suggest a diaphragm, a step toward the mammalian way of breathing.
The oldest frog-like animal known: a ten-centimetre salientian of the Early Triassic, with a frog's skull but still a short tail and a long back.
An abundant tusked herbivore whose disappearance defines the terrestrial extinction horizon in the Karoo.
A small, lizard-shaped diapsid of the latest Permian, close to the common ancestor of lizards and archosaurs; young were found huddled together in a burrow.
The earliest well-known cynodont, from the Late Permian of the Karoo, Zambia and Germany, with a paddle-like tail that suggests it swam.
A tongue-leaved seed fern blanketing Gondwana, whose distribution across five now-separate continents was early evidence for continental drift.
taxa.hb: woody tree in very wet soils, like a modern bald cypress; conical, widely spaced crowns to exploit low-angle polar light

taxa.note: The segmented root of the Glossopteris trees, preserved in Antarctic peat and Indian coal: the plumbing of a forest that grew in polar light.
taxa.hb: septate, air-filled roots in waterlogged soil

taxa.note: A strap-leaved cordaitalean of the Glossopteris flora, growing beside the seed ferns in the cool-temperate forests of Permian Gondwana.
A sabre-toothed predator of the Late Permian Karoo, top of the food chain before the Great Dying.
A wolf-sized gorgonopsian with long sabre canines, the kind of predator that hunted dicynodonts across the Late Permian Karoo.
A cow-sized, armour-studded plant-eater with leaf-shaped teeth -- one of the pareiasaurs, the largest herbivores of the Late Permian.
A slender sphenopsid with wedge-shaped leaves in whorls, a scrambling plant of Carboniferous and Permian swamps on every continent.
A bear-sized gorgonopsian with sabre teeth, the apex predator of the last Permian ecosystems.
taxa.hb: terrestrial apex predator with sabre canines

taxa.note: A boomerang-headed amphibian of Permian ponds, its skull drawn out into broad lateral horns.
A two-metre, flat-headed temnospondyl of the Late Permian rivers -- one of the big amphibians that the end-Permian extinction nearly ended.
A thick-skulled, barrel-chested dinocephalian of the Karoo: a three-metre herbivore built for head-butting.
A horsetail with unbranched stems, the Angaran and Gondwanan counterpart of Calamites, along every Permian riverbank of Siberia and the Glossopteris country.
The commonest large animal of the middle Permian Karoo, a two-and-a-half-metre pareiasaur with a warty hide, in herds on the floodplain.
A large dicynodont with rows of cheek teeth, found from the Karoo to India and Brazil: one of the animals that show Permian Gondwana was one country.
Sabre-toothed therapsid predators with an erect gait -- the first mammal-line animals that hunt like mammals.
A freshwater shark with an eel's body and a long spine at the back of the head, hunting the coal-swamp rivers and lakes for a hundred million years.
Stocky lizard-shaped early reptiles, some with several rows of teeth for grinding plants -- among the first small herbivores on land.
