Massive, thick-skulled therapsids, likely head-butting, that go extinct at the end of the interval.
An early conifer of Permian Gondwana, in the Parana and Karoo basins as the ice withdrew.
A small aquatic reptile of Permian Gondwanan lakes, found on matching shores in Brazil and South Africa - Wegener's evidence for drift.
A eurypterid of the Permian of Brazil, one of the last of its kind, in the rivers and lakes of Gondwana.
An early conifer in drier upland settings -- the beginning of forest that is not a swamp.
A small mesosaur of the Irati and Whitehill shales, in the inland sea shared by Brazil and South Africa before the Atlantic; with Mesosaurus, early evidence for drift.
Cockroaches and their roachoid forerunners -- the commonest insects of the coal forests, and unhurried ever since.
A cold-climate seed plant of the floras that recolonised bare ground as the Karoo ice sheets melted.
Cold marine faunas in the seas around a Gondwana buried under Carboniferous ice.
A small tree lycopsid of Carboniferous Argentina, growing in the outwash plains in front of Gondwana's glaciers.
The seed fern that marks the Permian red beds across Euramerica: the flora of a continent that had lost its swamps.
Giant predatory lobe-finned fish of the Carboniferous rivers of Laurussia.
Seed ferns with enormous fronds and the largest seeds of the Palaeozoic.
A fern-like seed plant of Carboniferous Gondwana, the commonest fossil of the cold country between the ice sheets; its name is a flora as much as a plant.
A fern-like seed plant with fan-shaped leaflets, the signature plant of the Early Carboniferous of eastern Australia and Argentina.
An early tree lycopsid of Mississippian Gondwana and North Africa, before Lepidodendron proper.
An early horsetail of the Mississippian wetlands, ancestral to the giant Calamites that would build the coal swamps.
A giant sweep-feeding sea scorpion as long as a person, which raked lake and river beds with its spined limbs; one of its walking trackways runs six metres across a Scottish sandstone.
A thirty-metre lycopsid that grew fast, reproduced once and toppled -- the principal ingredient of coal.
taxa.hb: unbranched pole with a crown, DETERMINATE growth - grew, reproduced once, died

taxa.note: A small placoderm with a tall crest on its trunk armour, in fresh water from Greenland to Antarctica and Australia: the first fish genus shown to span both hemispheres.
A porolepiform lobe-finned fish up to two and a half metres long, with big rounded scales and fangs -- one of the commonest large fishes of Late Devonian rivers.
The first plant with a woody trunk and a true leafy canopy -- effectively the first modern-looking tree.
taxa.hb: the first true forest tree: real wood, roots to ~1 m, a spreading crown

taxa.note: A Late Devonian tree lycopsid with bark patterned in diamonds -- one of the few trees found across Gondwana and the northern continents alike.
Early sparse vegetation of horsetails and progymnosperms on the southern floodplains.
A Late Devonian tetrapod known from a jaw found in New South Wales, the first sign that the earliest four-limbed animals were in Gondwana as well as in Greenland.
An antiarch placoderm so abundant and widespread it is effectively the index fossil of Devonian fresh water.
A brachiopod that marks the Devonian seas of the Americas, from the Appalachian basin to the cool southern shelves.
The Gilboa tree: a trunk topped by a frond crown, and the oldest known forest stand.
taxa.hb: palm-like crown of frond-like branches

taxa.note: A Middle Devonian clubmoss with hooked leaf tips for climbing, known from New York to Australia: one of the first plants to spread across both hemispheres.
A sprawling Devonian lycopsid with sickle-shaped leaves, among the first plants with true leaves, on the shores of Laurussia and China alike.
The oldest fossil of a land organism with cord-forming mycelium. Fungi were rotting and binding the first soils before there were plant roots to put in them.
The Bokkeveld Group and Parana Basin preserve the cold-water Devonian brachiopod-trilobite province.
The Middle Devonian fishes of the Aztec Siltstone in the Transantarctic Mountains -- placoderms, acanthodians, lungfish and early sharks in rivers and lakes at 30 degrees south.
Ringed, tapering shells a centimetre long, in such numbers that they pave Devonian bedding planes; what the animal was is still argued.
A small, disc-shaped tabulate coral colony that often grew around a worm living in its base.
Green algae established in shallow water; the ancestors of every land plant are somewhere in this group.
Red algae persist through the glaciations in shallow refugia.

Smooth-walled spheres without ornament, a form genus that holds the resting cysts of countless Proterozoic and Palaeozoic algae; in the Cryogenian, after the spiny acritarchs died back, they are most of what the seas left.
A conodont genus of a hundred species that carries the Devonian time scale, from the Rhenish shelf to Guangxi.
The Petoskey stone: a colonial rugose coral of Devonian reefs whose six-sided corallites turn up as pebbles on Lake Michigan beaches.
A spiriferide brachiopod of the cold Malvinokaffric shelves of southern Gondwana.
A few centimetres of leafless forking stem with a spore capsule on top: the first vascular plant, and the ancestor of every forest.
taxa.hb: tiny dichotomising axes in damp lowlands

taxa.note: A lycophyte with real leaves, appearing surprisingly early in Australia and complicating every tidy story about plant evolution.
taxa.hb: creeping and upright shoots with true microphylls

taxa.note: The lace bryozoan, a fan of branches joined by crossbars, on Carboniferous and Permian sea floors from Australia to the Urals.
A trilobite with a broad, fan-shaped, ribbed tail shield -- a characteristic dweller of Silurian and Devonian reefs.
A trilobite with towering eyes crowned by a sunshade -- evidence that it lived in bright, shallow water.
A wide, flat-coiled euomphalid sea snail of Devonian to Permian shelves, grazing the reef flats of the Rhenish Massif and the Urals.
A 'sun coral', a tabulate whose tubes stand in a honeycomb of finer ones, building Silurian and Devonian reefs with Favosites and Halysites.
One of the first ammonoids, a small coiled goniatite of the Emsian seas of Morocco and the Rhenish shelf: the beginning of a lineage that lasted 340 million years.
An orthide brachiopod of the cold Malvinokaffric seas of Silurian and Devonian Gondwana: Bolivia, Brazil, the Falklands and South Africa.
A Devonian plant known from spore capsules on short stalks, close to the mosses; found in Belgium, China and Australia.
A giant eurypterid with grasping claws, one of the largest arthropods that ever lived.
taxa.hb: nektonic sea scorpion with crushing chelicerae

taxa.note: The commonest conodont of Silurian seas, whose apparatus is known entire; its species date the Silurian on every shelf.
Millipede-grade arthropods, among the first animals to live permanently out of water.
Bony fishes, which split early into ray-fins and lobe-fins; one branch of the lobe-fins leads to everything with four limbs.
Sea scorpions, in decline for a hundred million years, finally gone.
A distinctive low-diversity cold-water shelly province across South America, South Africa and the Falklands.
An index brachiopod of the cool Silurian Malvinokaffric seas, unlike anything in the tropics.
Liverwort-grade plants -- the first land vegetation, known from cryptospores rather than bodies.
A small, ribbed bivalve of the Silurian, abundant in the dark limestones of Bohemia and North Africa.
Sessile on carbonate shelves
taxa.hb: sessile on carbonate shelves

taxa.note: Heat- and sulphur-loving microbes at the base of food webs run entirely on chemistry, not light.
Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, found inside the earliest land plants. Those plants had no roots, so the fungus was the root; the partnership still runs about eighty percent of plant species today.
Vase-shaped microfossils -- testate amoebae that built shells and, by implication, had something to hide from.
Biological soil crust binding sand between rains, the desert's living skin.
A trilobite with a long tail spine and large crescent eyes, a swimmer or fast crawler of the Silurian shelf.
The 'Dudley bug', a trilobite so abundant in the Silurian limestone of the English Midlands that the town put it on its coat of arms.
A large, smooth homalonotid trilobite with a triangular head, which ploughed through the Silurian and Devonian mud.
Single-celled prokaryotes with no nucleus, forming the mats and stromatolites that dominate the fossil record for most of Earth's history.
A disc-shaped phosphatic brachiopod that fastened to shells and driftwood, thriving in the oxygen-poor muds of the Gondwanan Devonian.
The type hyolith: a cone-shaped shell with a lid, and a pair of curved struts it steered with, on sea floors from the Cambrian to the Permian.
A calcified dasyclad alga, a branching tube a few millimetres wide, that paved shallow Ordovician and Silurian carbonate floors on every continent.
A calcified dasyclad of Late Ordovician and Silurian shelves, one of the algae that turned Silurian lagoons into limestone.
A wide, gently curved strophomenide with a straight hinge, resting on the sediment on its convex valve, on every Ordovician and Silurian shelf.
Single-row graptolites that swarm Silurian seas, evolving so fast that they date the rocks they drift into.
A wrinkled, flat-lying brachiopod with a sharp bend at the edge, one of the longest-lived shell genera of the Palaeozoic.
Jawless armoured fish, bottom-feeding and slow, and the only vertebrates in the water.
Robust, strongly enrolling trilobites that dominate the cold high-latitude Ordovician shelves where reefs are absent.
Colonial, honeycomb corallites
taxa.hb: colonial, honeycomb corallites

taxa.note: Tillite: the unsorted rubble a glacier leaves, cemented to rock. Gondwana's Carboniferous-Permian tillites lie on five continents, and their scratched pavements were among the first evidence that those continents had once been one.
The conodont animal preserved whole: forty centimetres long, eel-like, with big eyes and muscle blocks, from a shale laid down under the end-Ordovician ice.
A phacopid with a pointed tail that lived through the Hirnantian glaciation: the trilobite of the cold-water Hirnantia fauna from Bohemia and Wales to Morocco and Bolivia.
The organ-pipe coral: loose bundles of tubes joined by cross-bars, from the Silurian to the Permian on every continent, common in Carboniferous reefs.
A cold-water brachiopod assemblage that spread worldwide as end-Ordovician ice gripped the Saharan pole.
A trinucleid with a wide pitted fringe, named for the Onny valley of Shropshire and sold by the thousand from the Ordovician of Morocco.
A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, metres long, hunting the Ordovician carbonate platform.
A spiny acritarch -- the resting cyst of an Ordovician plankter -- used to date the Ordovician rocks of Baltica.
A colonial coral (or perhaps an alga) of the Ordovician with tubes divided into four, forming mounds in the warm lagoons of Laurentia and Siberia.
A three-to-six-pointed star of an acritarch, the resting cyst of a Palaeozoic plankter, found in marine rocks from the Ordovician to the Permian.
A calymenid trilobite of the cold, muddy shelves that ringed high-latitude Gondwana.
A peri-Gondwanan acritarch with long branching spines, a marker of the cold high-latitude Ordovician seas off North Africa and Iberia.
The straight-shelled nautiloid of the Baltic 'Orthoceras limestone', a metre-long swimmer whose chambered shells pave the floors of Swedish churches.
A jawless armoured fish of Ordovician Gondwana, tadpole-shaped with a bony head shield, in shoals along the Bolivian shore.
Tiny calcified rods, probably a green alga, that make up much of the Early Ordovician lime sands of Laurentia and Siberia.
The orthide that named its order: a ribbed, straight-hinged brachiopod of Ordovician shelves from Baltica and Laurentia to the Gondwanan margin.
A large asaphid of the Darriwilian shelf of Bolivia and northern Argentina, the commonest trilobite of the Andean Ordovician.
One of the oldest fishes with a bony skeleton: a jawless, finless, armoured swimmer of the Early Ordovician sea over central Australia.
Moroccan mudstones extend Burgess-type soft-bodied preservation into the Ordovician of the Saharan shelf.
A smooth illaenid of the Mediterranean province, tucked into the sediment with only its convex head showing, in Bohemia, Portugal, Morocco and Wales.
Colonial corals with honeycomb skeletons, joining stromatoporoids as reef builders.
A two-metre radiodont that filtered plankton with comb-like head limbs -- the gentle giant of the Early Ordovician Fezouata sea.
A Tremadocian trilobite with a broad spiny pygidium, of the Argentine Cordillera Oriental, the Tinu Formation of Oaxaca and the Laurentian shelf.
The olenid that marks the base of the Ordovician in Argentina and Bolivia, Oaxaca, Nevada, Kazakhstan and Norway: a wide-ranging trilobite of the outer shelf.
A burrowing brachiopod that survives everything and looks much the same today.
A shrub-like calcified microbe that framed reefs with the archaeocyaths in the Cambrian and again in the Late Devonian.
The conodont whose first appearance at Green Point, Newfoundland, defines the base of the Ordovician.
An olenid trilobite of the Furongian black shales -- the Alum Shale of Scandinavia, Wales, Argentina and Oaxaca -- living at the edge of oxygen on the sea floor.
Large, smooth-shelled trilobites, some with eyes on stalks, that dominate many Ordovician carbonate platforms.
A late Cambrian trilobite of Shandong and the North China platform, whose pustular shell names a zone of the Chinese Furongian.
A late Cambrian trilobite of the outer shelves of Cathaysia, Kazakhstan, Australia and Siberia, with a broad flat pygidium; a zone fossil of the Furongian on the Gondwanan and Asian side.
An agnostoid of the last Cambrian stage, proposed to define its base, from Quebec and Nevada to Kazakhstan, Australia and China.
The earliest articulate brachiopods, ribbed and nearly symmetrical, abundant on Ordovician shelves.
A long-lived agnostoid of the late Cambrian and earliest Ordovician, on shelves everywhere; the last common agnostoid before the group dwindled.
Clotted microbial mounds build reefs across the vast, nearly flat epicontinental sea.
The agnostoid whose first appearance at Duibian in Zhejiang defines the base of the Jiangshanian stage, found from Kazakhstan and Siberia to Laurentia.
A net-patterned agnostoid whose first appearance in Hunan defines the base of the Paibian and the Furongian series; found on every continent, the standard of the late Cambrian.
A tiny blind agnostid trilobite that drifted worldwide, which is what makes it the middle Cambrian's best time-marker.
A thin-walled glass sponge whose cross-shaped spicules lie in rows, in Cambrian and Ordovician shales from the Burgess Shale to Wales and China.
A paradoxidid of the Cambrian of Bohemia, Spain, Morocco and Scandinavia, with a long spiny pygidium; a zone fossil of the middle Cambrian across the Gondwanan and Baltic shelves.
A kutorginid brachiopod of the Burgess Shale and the Laurentian shelf, sometimes preserved with its spines still attached.
A blind trilobite of the Cambrian mud floors of Bohemia, the Montagne Noire, Spain, Wales and Morocco: eyes were of no use in the dark water it lived in.
A metre-long swimming predator with grasping appendages, and the first animal large enough to sit at the top of a food web.
taxa.hb: active nektonic swimmer with lateral flaps

taxa.note: A large spiny trilobite of the Baltic-Avalonian 'Atlantic' province, unknown on Cambrian Laurentia.
A blind agnostoid a few millimetres long, head and tail nearly identical, drifting or crawling on Cambrian sea floors worldwide; in the Wheeler Shale it is the commonest fossil of all.
A bivalved Cambrian arthropod with big stalked eyes and spines fore and aft -- a swimming predator found in almost every Cambrian Lagerstätte.
A trilobite a hand-span long from the Cambrian of Morocco, the commonest large fossil of the Jbel Wawrmast beds and of the fossil trade.
A large, spiny redlichiid trilobite that typifies the Cambrian shelves of Gondwana and China.
taxa.hb: benthic

taxa.note: A cup-shaped reef builder of the early Cambrian, sponge-grade animals that made the first animal reefs and were gone by the middle of the period.
A South Australian Lagerstatte where Anomalocaris keeps its compound eyes - tens of thousands of lenses each.
A calcified microbe growing as clusters of tiny chambered lumps -- a builder of reefs beside the archaeocyath sponges in the Cambrian and the stromatoporoids in the Devonian.
One of the first trilobites of Morocco's Anti-Atlas, a fallotaspidoid of the Issafen Formation, near the base of the trilobite record on the Gondwanan shelf.
A slug-shaped animal armoured with two thousand sclerites and a shell at each end, known whole from Sirius Passet in Greenland and from its scattered sclerites on most early Cambrian shelves.
Among the first trilobites anywhere: a flat, wide-headed olenelloid of the Anti-Atlas of Morocco and the Fallotaspis zone of Nevada and California, at the base of the trilobite record.
The tommotiid that named the Tommotian stage of Siberia: asymmetric phosphatic caps, paired left and right, that armoured a sessile animal on the earliest Cambrian sea floor.
A lobopodian whose net-patterned armour plates were known as small shelly fossils for decades before the Chengjiang animal that wore them turned up.
Small conical Cambrian shells with a lid and a pair of props. What they actually were was argued for 175 years -- probably relatives of brachiopods.
A bag-shaped animal armoured with star-shaped spicules, sessile on Cambrian sea floors, whose isolated stars are among the commonest small shelly fossils.
A slender phosphatic tube a few millimetres long, once taken for a hyolith and now for the dwelling of a worm, on Cambrian shelves everywhere.
Conical phosphatic sclerites with ribbed sides, the armour of a tommotiid, a lophophorate that wore a coat of them; among the commonest small shelly fossils of the early Cambrian.

A tiny laterally compressed shell, a mollusc near the root of the bivalves and rostroconchs, whose first appearance is the candidate marker for the second stage of the Cambrian from Siberia to Newfoundland and China.
A three-lobed tube a few millimetres long, among the first mineralised skeletons of the Cambrian and a zone fossil of its opening stage on every continent.
A tiny coiled shell of the earliest Cambrian, snail-like or a mollusc's cousin, found from Siberia to Newfoundland and marking the base of the Tommotian.

Curved phosphatic spines a millimetre long, the grasping teeth of an arrow-worm-like animal, and the first tooth-shaped fossils of the Cambrian: Protohertzina anabarica marks the Fortunian on every continent.
The zigzag burrow that defines the base of the Cambrian: an animal probing the sediment from below, worldwide, at a level no body fossil can match.
Sponges. Molecular clocks and disputed biomarkers place their origin in the Tonian or Cryogenian; unambiguous body fossils come later.
Shelled filter feeders that will dominate the shelf benthos for the next three hundred million years.
A fractal frondose Ediacaran of the Namibian shelf, type of the whole rangeomorph group.
A tube of nested layers, a centimetre long, from the last Ediacaran of South China, Nevada and Brazil: one of the first animals with a mineral skeleton, beside Cloudina.
A goblet-shaped skeletal organism from the Nama Group, part of the first mineralised reef community.
taxa.hb: stalked, attached to microbial reefs

taxa.note: A ribbon-shaped fossil with fine transverse rings, from the last Ediacaran of Shaanxi and India to the first Cambrian: an animal or a colony, and a marker of the boundary interval.
Partly buried, sack-like, in shifting sand
taxa.hb: partly buried, sack-like, in shifting sand

taxa.note: An erniettomorph of the Nama Group, a bag of tubular segments that lived half-buried in the shifting sand of the last Ediacaran shelves.
A four-sided organic tube with a mineral coat from the Tamengo Formation of Brazil, also in Nevada: read as a stalked cnidarian, a scyphozoan polyp fixed to the last Ediacaran sea floor.
The holdfast disc of Newfoundland's Fermeuse Formation, the first Ediacaran fossil ever named (1872) and dismissed for a century; thousands cover some bedding planes.

Ribbon-shaped carbonaceous compressions a millimetre wide and centimetres long, on Ediacaran bedding planes from the White Sea to South China: an alga or a sulphur bacterium, and among the commonest fossils of the age.
Chains of repeating chambers on Ediacaran bedding planes, once taken for a trail and now for the body of a giant protist growing chamber by chamber, worldwide.
An encrusting skeletal organism up to a metre across that lined fissures in the Nama Group reefs of Namibia: the largest of the first animals with mineral skeletons.
Stacked calcareous cones that built the first animal reefs, and carry the first drill holes made by a predator.
taxa.hb: gregarious tube-dweller, reef-forming

taxa.note: Sheaths of a filamentous cyanobacterium, the mat-builder of Proterozoic tidal flats, preserved in chert on every craton.
A sac-like Ediacaran body with a lobed base, from the Flinders Ranges, read as a sea-anemone-like animal buried in life position.
A segmented Ediacaran form with a shield-like head end, argued over for decades as a possible early arthropod relative.
A disc with five-fold symmetry from the Flinders Ranges, the earliest candidate echinoderm.
A shield-shaped animal a centimetre long with an anchor-shaped ridge, from the Flinders Ranges and the White Sea, that could orient itself to the current.
Frond-shaped rangeomorphs anchored to the sea floor, feeding without a mouth or a gut.
taxa.hb: sessile frond anchored by a holdfast, in the deep sea below the photic zone

taxa.note: Found with a trail of its own feeding impressions.
taxa.hb: mobile grazer on microbial mats

taxa.note: A frond on a stalk with a holdfast disc, standing in the current from Newfoundland to the Flinders Ranges; the disc was found first and named alone.
Concentric discs pressed into Ediacaran sandstones on every continent, named as a jellyfish and now read as the holdfasts of fronds and the marks of microbial colonies.
Spiny organic-walled microfossils that make the Doushantuo a global Ediacaran reference.

A carbonaceous disc a few millimetres across, among the commonest large fossils of the Proterozoic, from the Grand Canyon to the Vindhyan of India: the compressed remains of a large-celled eukaryote or a colony.
The engine of the whole biosphere: oxygen producers and the builders of stromatolite reefs for well over a billion years.
A spiny acritarch of the early Ediacaran seas, one of the zone fossils of the Doushantuo-Pertatataka palynoflora; possibly the resting cysts of early animals.
A colonial coccoid cyanobacterium of Proterozoic cherts, all but identical to the living Entophysalis of tropical tidal flats.
A large acritarch with long branching processes, a signature of the early Ediacaran plankton after the Marinoan ice, from South China to central Australia and Siberia.
A sausage-shaped carbonaceous compression a centimetre long, found with Chuaria in Tonian and Ediacaran shales worldwide; read as a macroalga or a coenocytic organism.
Sheets of carbonate laid straight on top of glacial debris as a snowball Earth ended, under an atmosphere carrying hundreds of times today's CO2.
The cap carbonate laid over the Sturtian glacial deposits of the Otavi Group of Namibia: roll-up microbial mats metres thick, the first life of the sea floor after the snowball ice withdrew.
A slender, fast mosasaur of shallow water, the smallest of the Kansas chalk mosasaurs at two to four metres.
A mid-sized mosasaur, the commonest in the Kansas chalk, preserved with skin, a forked tail fin and the contents of its gut.
A stalkless crinoid that drifted in colonies of hundreds and sank together, leaving slabs of the Kansas chalk covered in its arms.
A cone-shaped larger foraminifer of the Urgonian reefs and platforms, the rock-former of the Aptian-Albian Tethys.
A large keeled Albian ammonite of the Tethys, Africa and the Americas, the last zone fossil of the Early Cretaceous.
A seven-metre pliosaur of the Early Jurassic, with nostrils built to smell under water, from the same Yorkshire and Somerset shales as Dactylioceras.
The Whitby ammonite, ribbed and evolute, once carved with snakes' heads and sold as the serpents St Hilda turned to stone.
Streamlined, live-bearing marine reptiles; Mary Anning's Lyme Regis specimens are how the world learned they existed.
Long-necked, four-flippered marine reptiles rowing through shallow Jurassic seas.
The smooth ammonite whose first appearance defines the base of the Jurassic, in the first seas after the end-Triassic extinction.
Thick heart-shaped bivalves crowding the Triassic Tethyan carbonate platforms.
A conodont whose platform elements zone the Permian and Triassic worldwide; the last of the conodonts went with its family at the end of the Triassic.
A Late Triassic spiriferinid brachiopod of the Panthalassan shelves, from Nevada to Peru.
The 'Rhaetic bone bed' bivalve, small and asymmetric, crowding the last sea floors of the Triassic in Europe.
The ammonoid group that radiated through the Triassic from the handful of lineages that survived the end-Permian bottleneck.
A thin flat 'paper clam' blanketing deep Tethyan Triassic seafloors along the drifting blocks.
A flat, paper-thin bivalve of Triassic deep-shelf muds, often found in mass-mortality pavements.
A small pearl-oyster relative of the Cassian beds of the Dolomites, where a whole Triassic reef community is preserved shell by shell.
Meadows of stalked crinoids ('sea lilies') whose disarticulated ossicles make crinoidal limestone.
An Early Triassic conodont whose elements date the recovery from the end-Permian extinction, stage by stage, in Pakistan, China and Nevada alike.
A metre-long early ichthyosaur with a fish's tail only half formed, from the Middle Triassic of the Alps, China and Nevada.
One of the earliest ichthyosaurs: within a few million years of the extinction, reptiles are already back in the sea.
A thin-shelled bivalve that carpets post-extinction seafloors -- the classic disaster taxon.
Leaf-like calcareous algae that grew in thickets on Pennsylvanian and Permian sea floors and built mounds hundreds of metres across -- the reef builders of an age with few corals.
A latest-Permian fusulinid whose disappearance pinpoints the marine mass extinction.
A rugose coral of Permian Tethyan reefs, colonial and thickly walled.
An athyridid brachiopod of the Permian of the Salt Range and the Himalayan margin, the commonest shell of the Tethyan shelf of India.
The last ammonoid of the Permian in Transcaucasia and Iran, its beds ending at the extinction horizon.
Rice-grain foraminifera, abundant and fast-evolving enough to date the Carboniferous limestones they largely consist of.
A Late Permian ammonoid with complex sutures on the road to the ammonites proper, from the Tethyan reefs of Timor.
A spiny productid brachiopod of the cool Permian seas of eastern Australia, the commonest fossil of the Sydney Basin marine beds.
A green alga built of chains of calcified beads, one of the main sediment-makers of the Permian reef lagoons, from the Capitan reef of Texas to the Tethys.
A small spiriferide brachiopod with a high flat beak, from the Silurian to the last Triassic sea floors.
A small, plain clam of low-oxygen Triassic muds, tolerant enough to be almost the only shell in some Early Triassic beds.
Silica-shelled plankton whose ooze hardens into the deep-sea cherts that record vanished ocean floors.
A trigoniid clam, ribbed and triangular, that burrowed the Triassic sands of the Tethys and the Muschelkalk sea.
A giant ichthyosaur reaching twenty metres, comparable to a modern large whale.
taxa.hb: pelagic

taxa.note: A thin-shelled bivalve that drifted or lay in shoals over the whole Late Triassic ocean; its beds date Norian rocks from Alaska to New Zealand.
A smooth, involute Late Triassic ammonoid of the Tethys and Timor, with fine spiral lines and sutures like lace.
A knobbly ceratitid ammonoid of the Carnian, in the Alps and the Tethys; its extinction near the Carnian Pluvial Episode.
A smooth, globular ceratitid ammonoid of the Middle Triassic Tethys, in the Alpine limestones by the thousand.
The sea lily of the Muschelkalk, whose stem ossicles make whole beds of the German Middle Triassic; the crinoid gardens of a shallow inland sea.
The ammonoid whose first appearance defines the base of the Triassic.
Palaeozoic ammonoids with zigzag sutures, abundant in the open water above Devonian to Permian shelves and basins.
An endemic clam of the Permian Passa Dois seaway of Brazil, an inland sea of Gondwana that had its own molluscs and nothing else's.
A cool-water strophalosiid brachiopod of Permian eastern Australia, cemented to the sea floor by its spines.
A spiriferide brachiopod of the Gondwanan cool-water Permian, from Queensland to Antarctica.
A small solitary horn coral of Pennsylvanian and Permian shelves, standing alone in the mud between the brachiopod beds.
A spiriferide brachiopod of the Permian Tethys, from the reefs of Tunisia to the Cathaysian shelves.
A flat, fan-shaped brachiopod of the Permian shelves of the Tethys and the Urals.
A leafy calcareous red alga that grew in thickets on Pennsylvanian shelves, building the 'phylloid algal mounds' that now hold oil.
A bryozoan built as a corkscrew: a lacy fan wound round a spiral axis, named for the screw, and a rock-former in Mississippian limestones.
A crinoid with a twisted stem and a low cup, from the Mississippian crinoid gardens of Indiana and Iowa where sea lilies grew in meadows.
A blastoid: a bud-shaped echinoderm on a stalk, with five feeding grooves, so abundant in the Mississippian of the Mississippi valley that they are sold by the jar.
A mosasaur over twelve metres long, the apex predator of the seaway that split North America.
A four-metre sea turtle, the largest ever, cruising the warm inland sea.
Dinoflagellates: armoured plankton whose resting cysts are the sea's fine-grained clock, and whose symbionts make a reef coral's colour and food.
A large disc-shaped foraminifer of Palaeogene tropical shelves, whose tests build limestone.
A small clam so abundant and fast-evolving it dates the whole boreal Jurassic-Cretaceous.
taxa.hb: cool-water shelf, gregarious

taxa.note: A large, late ichthyosaur found world-wide in Early Cretaceous seas; some Australian specimens are preserved as opal.
The grey wolf, once the most widely distributed wild land mammal on Earth.
Totora, the giant bulrush of Lake Titicaca from which the Uros build boats and floating islands.
The jaguar, the Americas' largest cat and the forest's apex predator.
Rattlesnakes, a New World invention: pit vipers with a warning rattle of interlocking keratin.
Twelve metres, eight tonnes, and the hardest bite of any land animal known. It lived only on Laramidia, the western island of a divided North America.
A horned dinosaur with a long, heart-shaped frill framing skin-covered windows -- a display structure rather than a shield.
A lighter, longer-legged tyrannosaur, the commonest big predator in one of the richest dinosaur faunas known.
A helmet-crested duckbill nine metres long; mummified skeletons keep the imprint of its pebbly skin.
Small mammaliaforms with complex molars, exploiting insect and plant food in the dinosaurs' shadow.
Twenty-six metres long and most of it neck and tail; peg teeth at the front of the jaw raked leaves off branches it never chewed.
A turiasaurian sauropod of the latest Jurassic of eastern Spain, some thirty metres long and perhaps forty tonnes -- one of the largest animals ever to live in Europe.
A chipmunk-sized burrowing mammal of the Late Jurassic with simple peg teeth like an aardvark's -- probably a digger into insect nests.
A stegosaur with a neck of at least seventeen vertebrae -- longer for its body than some sauropods' -- from the Late Jurassic of Portugal.
Turtles: ribs turned into a box. On land, in rivers and at sea since the Late Triassic.
A six-metre sauropodomorph named 'mouse lizard' for its tiny hatchlings; nest sites with eggs and young of many ages show it lived in herds.
Crocodile-shaped archosaurs lurking in Late Triassic rivers before crocodiles proper existed.
A toothless, beaked, two-legged reptile of the crocodile line that looks exactly like an ostrich dinosaur -- 80 million years before the ostrich dinosaurs.
Weasel- to wolf-sized therapsid predators. Unlike the gorgonopsians they got through the end-Permian extinction and hunted the Early Triassic.
A Late Permian reptiliomorph of the Angaran wetlands, close to the ancestry of amniotes.
A Cathaysian plant with two rows of leaves of two sizes, of uncertain kinship; it grew in the wet Permian forests of China and nowhere else.
Strap-leaved coniferophytes up to thirty metres tall on the drier ground beyond the mires: the first vegetation that would read as forest rather than swamp.
taxa.hb: tree with strap-shaped leaves; coastal and upland

taxa.note: A Cathaysian seed plant with broad net-veined leaves that look startlingly like an angiosperm's, 150 million years early.
taxa.hb: climbing or scrambling, with large net-veined leaves

taxa.note: A pareiasaur of the Late Permian of Shanxi, a barrel-bodied plant-eater armoured with bony studs.
The pareiasaur of Kotelnich, known from dozens of skeletons, a plant-eater the size of a cow.
A horsetail relative with whorls of broad leaves, characteristic of the Cathaysian flora.
A Cathaysian seed fern with netted leaf veins, of the Permian coal swamps of North China.
A heavily built pareiasaur from the Russian Permian, knobbly-skulled and barrel-bodied.
A pig-sized dicynodont that dug spiral burrows in the Karoo floodplain; the most abundant vertebrate fossil of the Late Permian of South Africa.
A carnivorous dinocephalian two and a half metres long, with long canines and a heavy skull -- a top predator of the Middle Permian before the gorgonopsians took over.
Barrel-bodied synapsids with absurdly small heads: Cotylorhynchus reached four metres and was the first really large plant-eater on land.
Long-bodied, eel-like reptiliomorphs of the coal-swamp pools -- fish-eating ambush predators close to the ancestry of amniotes.
Extinct beaked insects with a third pair of winglets, sucking on Carboniferous plant reproductive organs.
A small early reptile with chewing teeth, of the Permian of Texas and, as its relative Belebey, of Russia and China.
A sail-backed synapsid predator, more closely related to us than to any dinosaur, and routinely mis-sold as one.
taxa.hb: terrestrial apex predator with a tall neural-spine sail

taxa.note: The largest land animal of its day: a caseid with a body like a barrel and a head that looks borrowed from something a tenth its size.
A stocky, armour-backed amphibian with a large eardrum notch -- a land-going temnospondyl of the Early Permian, probably active at night.
An early sail-backed synapsid, and one of the first large herbivorous land vertebrates.
A lightly built, monitor-like synapsid predator a metre and a half long -- one of the last of the early branch of the mammal line.
A lycopsid tree of the Cathaysian coal forests of South China -- the rainforests that kept growing after the Euramerican ones collapsed.
A heavy-bodied temnospondyl amphibian, effectively the crocodile of Permian rivers.
A two-metre millipede, the largest land arthropod that has ever existed, leaving trackways across swamp floors.
taxa.hb: ground-dwelling

taxa.note: A dragonfly relative with a wingspan approaching three-quarters of a metre, possible only in a high-oxygen atmosphere.
taxa.hb: aerial predator, ~70 cm wingspan

taxa.note: A forty-centimetre, long-limbed reptile of the latest Carboniferous, one of the first diapsids -- the line that later gave lizards, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds.
A tree fern whose trunk was a mantle of adventitious roots rather than wood. It took over the mires as the giant lycopsids faltered.
taxa.hb: tree fern with a mantle of adventitious roots

taxa.note: A palaeoniscoid ray-finned fish with heavy rhombic scales, the commonest fish of Carboniferous lagoons and coal-swamp lakes in Europe.
Produced the largest pollen grains known.
taxa.hb: scrambling or self-supporting, with very large fronds

taxa.note: One of the oldest synapsids, the line leading to mammals: a fifty-centimetre, lizard-shaped insect-eater found inside a fossil tree stump in Nova Scotia.
One of the first large plant-eaters on land: a three-metre, barrel-bodied tetrapod with broad cheek teeth, close to the ancestry of reptiles.
A palaeodictyopteran with patterned, net-veined wings and a beak for sucking plant juices, from the coal forests of France.
A ten-centimetre, salamander-shaped dissorophoid of the Pennsylvanian coal swamps, close to the ancestry of frogs and salamanders.
One of the first true reptiles, sheltering in hollow lycophyte stumps in Nova Scotia.
taxa.hb: insectivore living in hollow lycopsid stumps

taxa.note: A seven-metre freshwater lobe-finned predator, the largest freshwater fish known.
One of the oldest winged insects, a palaeodictyopteran from the Early Carboniferous -- flight had begun, 150 million years before any other animal flew.
A long-bodied colosteid with a flat skull and the lateral-line grooves of a fish -- an eel-like hunter that never really left the water.
A two-metre anthracosaur of the Mississippian, a long-bodied predator of the swamps from West Virginia to Scotland.
A Mississippian seed fern with finely divided, wedge-lobed fronds, among the first seed plants to spread across the continents.
A Mississippian scorpion some 35 centimetres long from the lake shores of Scotland -- one of the first scorpions certainly built for land.
Scale trees beginning their takeover of coastal mires -- the coal machine is warming up.
A small, slender East Kirkton tetrapod, close to the origin of fully terrestrial amniotes.
A 70 cm scorpion of the Scottish coal-age forests, with compound eyes and book lungs -- a land hunter, not a swimmer.
A small land-going temnospondyl with an eardrum -- among the first tetrapods that could hear sound travelling through air.
A slender twenty-centimetre tetrapod from a Mississippian lake shore in Scotland, once hailed as the earliest reptile and now placed just outside the amniotes.
A tall-spired sea snail of Triassic shelves, common enough in the Cassian and Muschelkalk faunas to be the Triassic's ordinary snail.
An early ichthyosaur up to seventeen metres long with an eel-like body and no dorsal fin, from Nevada's Middle Triassic sea.
A small long-necked marine reptile found by the thousand in Guizhou Triassic shales.
A planispiral snail-like mollusc, coiled in one plane like a tiny nautilus, grazing Carboniferous and Permian sea floors.
A smooth triangular clam of late Palaeozoic shelves, burrowing the Permian sands of the Zechstein and the Ural Ocean.
A spiny productid brachiopod, the commonest shell of the Permian Tethys from Transcaucasia to South China; its last species die at the boundary.
A small chonetid brachiopod with spines along the hinge, on Permian sea floors by the thousand, in South China above all.
The winged spiriferid brachiopod itself, broad and ribbed, of Carboniferous shelves the world over.
A small spiny productid brachiopod of the Carboniferous shelves of Europe and the Urals.
A Serpukhovian goniatite of the Ural Ocean, from the Dombar hills of Kazakhstan where the stage was named.
A colonial rugose coral in bundles of narrow tubes, the reef-builder of Mississippian limestones from Britain to the Sahara and North China.
A dasyclad green alga whose calcified branches make up part of many Mississippian limestones.
A twig-like bryozoan of late Palaeozoic shelves, its branches in every Permian limestone of Brazil and the Urals.
A scallop-like bivalve of the late Palaeozoic, in every shelf sea from the Mississippian to the end of the Permian.
A large solitary horn coral of Carboniferous shelves, standing a hand's length high in the mud of the Ural Ocean and the European shelves.
A large, high-beaked spiriferinid brachiopod of Mississippian shelves, from the Himalayan margin of India to Ireland.
A ribbed goniatite of the Tournaisian, in the black shales of the Sahara and the Rhenish shelf.
The conodont whose first appearance was chosen to mark the base of the Carboniferous, in the Tournaisian seas of China and Europe.
A smooth spiral-brachidium brachiopod with frilled growth lamellae, common in the Rhenish Devonian and the Ural Ocean's shelves.
A globular Late Devonian goniatite of the open shelf, from the Canning Basin of Australia to the Rhenish Massif.
A rounded, finely ribbed orthid brachiopod, one of the commonest shells of Devonian and Carboniferous shelves from Germany to China and Australia.
A shallow-water conodont of the Devonian, its rows of nodes the standard zonation of the near-shore seas from the Lochkovian to the Famennian.
A round, finely ribbed brachiopod with a spiral feeding organ inside, in nearly every Silurian and Devonian shelf sea in the world.
A Middle Devonian index fossil of the Old World Realm.
taxa.hb: benthic, attached

taxa.note: A small proetid trilobite of the Devonian of Morocco and the Rhenish shelf, the proetids being the family that would outlast every other trilobite.
The first spiriferide: a brachiopod with a coiled internal support for its feeding organ, from the last Ordovician to the Early Devonian, the start of a line that ran to the Jurassic.
A jawless fish covered in tiny tooth-like scales, known mostly from those scales, which pave Silurian sandstones from the Baltic to Arctic Canada and Siberia.
The oldest articulated bony fish, from the late Silurian Kuanti Formation of Yunnan: a lobe-finned fish with a mosaic of features the ray-fins and lobe-fins would later divide between them.
A placoderm from the Kuanti Formation of Yunnan with a bony jaw of the pattern all bony fishes and land vertebrates inherit; it moved the origin of the jaws we have into the armoured fishes.
A golf-ball alga: a sphere of packed branch-tips a few centimetres across, calcified, in Ordovician and Silurian limestones of Laurentia and Baltica.
A ray-finned fish of the Kupferschiefer copper-shale, preserved as the sea first flooded then stagnated.
Spiny, thick-shelled brachiopods resting on soft carbonate mud, the dominant shellfish of the late Paleozoic sea floor.
A calcified sponge of the Permian reefs of Tunisia, where sponges, not corals, built the reef.
A sphinctozoan sponge, a string of beads with a canal through them, one of the builders of the Permian Reef of Texas.
The first gliding reptile: a lizard-sized weigeltisaurid that spread wings of skin on rods of bone growing from its flanks.
Tree-sized horsetails forming dense stands along channel margins.
taxa.hb: clonal thickets on levees and channel margins

taxa.note: A peltasperm seed fern with long, tongue-shaped leaves, typical of the Late Permian floras of the Russian platform and Angara.
A small anomodont from Kotelnich with a grasping hand and long tail: the earliest tree-climbing vertebrate known.
The Late Permian tetrapods of Kotelnich on the Vyatka: pareiasaurs, gorgonopsians and the earliest cynodont-like therapsids, from a riverbank where they are found standing in their burrows.
Tall, usually unbranched, in coal swamps
taxa.hb: tall, usually unbranched, in coal swamps

taxa.note: A tetrapod so close to the amphibian-amniote boundary that its placement has flipped repeatedly.
A metre-long diadectid known from its skeleton and its own footprints -- enough to rebuild its gait as a robot, which showed it walked more upright than expected.
A two-to-three-metre synapsid with a long, deep skull -- probably a fish-eater of the Early Permian rivers and swamps.
A whip spider of the coal forests, with long raptorial forelegs -- the arachnid order has barely changed since.
A small horseshoe crab of the coal-swamp pools, with spined edges to its shield -- a freshwater cousin of the living Limulus.
A palaeodictyopteran with a wingspan of up to half a metre and a sucking beak, from the coal-swamp nodules of Illinois.
A scale tree of the coal swamps whose leaf cushions overlapped like the scales of a cone; it grew as one tall pole, branched once into a crown, shed its spores and died.
A scrambling seed fern with glandular hairs on its stems, one of the first plants whose seed-bearing life was worked out from fossils.
The wolverine: a mustelid that kills prey many times its size and caches it in the frozen ground.
The sable, whose fur drove the Russian conquest of Siberia.
Siberian spruce, the taiga's dominant tree across the range.
The capercaillie, the turkey-sized grouse of old conifer forest.
A squirrel-like relative of primates with big gnawing incisors -- one of the few Paleocene mammals found on both sides of the young North Atlantic.
One of the first turtles with a complete shell: a metre-long, toothless reptile with a spiked, clubbed tail, which could not yet pull its head in.
The Permian coal flora of the Kuznetsk Basin: Rufloria and Cordaites forests with Angaropteridium beneath them, the counterpart in cool Angara of the Glossopteris forests of the south.
The characteristic Angaran leaf - cool temperate, seasonal, deciduous.
taxa.hb: deciduous tree with strong growth rings

taxa.note: A gymnosperm of the Angaran flora, from a Permian Siberia too cold for the coal swamps of the tropics.
A bull-sized Russian dinocephalian carrying horn-like bosses on its skull -- a signature Angaran animal.
An Angaran seed fern, its fronds among the commonest plant fossils of the Kuznetsk Basin coal measures.
The American black bear, the range's largest surviving carnivore.
A two-metre sauropodomorph whose bones, found in 1818, were the first dinosaur skeleton discovered in North America -- though not recognised as one for decades.
Spider-like arachnids among the first land predators -- there was already something worth hunting.
One of the earliest seed plants; the seed is what eventually lets vegetation leave the water's edge.
taxa.hb: small woody plant

taxa.note: A fern-like plant of the latest Devonian that grew in dense thickets on floodplains -- and burned: charcoal from its wildfires is common in its beds.
A large predatory lobe-fin hunting in the same rivers as the first tetrapods, and eating them.

Tapering trunks up to eight metres tall standing over a landscape where nothing else reached the knee. Carbon isotopes point to a fungus rather than a plant, making it the largest organism on land for 40 million years.
taxa.hb: free-standing column, the tallest organism of its day

taxa.note: A Devonian relative of Arthropleura, an early millipede-grade detritivore of the first forest floors.
A lobe-finned fish with the limb bone arrangement of a tetrapod already inside its fin.
One of the oldest centipedes, known from its legs in the Rhynie chert and the Gilboa forest -- already a venomous hunter of the early undergrowth.
An early arachnid that made silk from spigots set in plates rather than spinnerets: silk long before webs.
The tree of the Gilboa 'forest' in New York - the oldest known forest, of fern-like Wattieza trees.
One of the earliest ray-finned fishes, a fast predator of the Devonian lakes of Scotland and Quebec, ancestral in form to half the vertebrates alive.
A half-metre arthrodire of the Old Red Sandstone lakes and seas of Scotland, armoured over the head and trunk and naked behind.
An early lycopsid of the Devonian of China and Europe, low and branching, before the tree forms of its group.
The Devonian trilobite of New York and Ohio, once called Phacops rana, whose eye lenses were read for the evolution of vision.
A small, smooth goniatite with a zigzag suture, one of the commonest ammonoids of the Middle and Late Devonian seas.
A cladoxylopsid tree from the oldest forest floors known. It shed whole branches rather than leaves, and its roots began cracking rock into soil and drawing CO2 out of the air.
A trimerophyte that grew a main stem with side branches in a spiral -- the first hint of the trunk-and-branch plan of trees.
A winged spiriferide brachiopod of the Middle Devonian Appalachian seas, its hinge drawn out into long points.
A spiny, leafless zosterophyll whose stems uncoiled like fern fiddleheads -- a cousin of the lycopods.
A trilobite with a broad, pitted horseshoe brim around its head -- probably a sieve for sifting food from the mud.
A spiny odontopleurid trilobite with two long horns curling back from its head like a ram's.
A bony-shielded jawless fish of Old Red Sandstone rivers and lakes.
A trimerophyte of the Early Devonian: leafless stems that forked and forked again to a metre tall -- the stock from which ferns, horsetails and seed plants branched.
The trilobite with the compound eyes of stacked calcite lenses, each one visible to the naked eye; a Devonian reef-dweller found enrolled by the hundred.
Fine calcified filaments that crusted over corals and stromatoporoids on the reefs of the Silurian and Devonian.
A two-metre pterygotid sea scorpion with long pincers, among the largest arthropods of the Silurian.
Sea scorpions patrolling brackish lagoons, some large enough to take vertebrate prey.
A chain coral: tubes joined side by side into ranks that wander across the rock like chain-link, on Late Ordovician and Silurian shelves everywhere.
A branching trepostome bryozoan of Ordovician and Silurian shelves, its twigs the commonest bryozoan debris of the Cincinnatian.
Sprawling, rhizomatous vascular plants that built the first vegetation dense enough to change how rivers behave.
A lichid the size of a dinner plate from the Rochester Shale of New York, one of the largest Silurian trilobites.
A Silurian crinoid whose arms fused into a web, a filtering fan; it grew in meadows on Silurian reefs.
A eurypterid with a scorpion-like curled tail and spined forelimbs, from the Ringerike sandstones of Norway; it walked as much as it swam.
A solitary horn coral, the simplest of the rugose corals, standing on its tip in the Ordovician mud.
A large pentamerid brachiopod of the Llandovery whose changing shape through time is used to date Silurian rocks.
A strongly ribbed brachiopod with a sharp fold, so common in Cincinnatian rocks that it is Ohio's state fossil in all but name.
A smooth illaenid of the Wenlock reefs of Dudley and Gotland and the Silurian of Laurentia, its head and tail nearly featureless domes.
A wide, flat strophomenid brachiopod that lay on the mud like a dropped coin, the most abundant shell in the Ordovician limestones of the American Midwest.
One of the largest trilobites.
taxa.hb: benthic burrower

taxa.note: The name-bearer of the cold-water brachiopod fauna that briefly took over the world's shelves during the glaciation.
A spiny cheirurid trilobite of the Trenton limestone seas, sometimes preserved with its legs.
One of the largest Ordovician sea scorpions, more than a metre long, with spiny grasping forelimbs.
A ribbed orthid brachiopod, one of the commonest shells of the Late Ordovician seas of Laurentia.
A ball-shaped dasyclad green alga of the Ordovician, like a small calcified sea-grape, common on the carbonate shelves of Laurentia and Baltica.
A calcified green alga of the Ordovician of Baltica and Laurentia, close to the living Halimeda in build, and a rock-former in Norway's Oslo region.
One of the oldest vertebrates with a skeleton, a jawless fish clad in mosaic bony plates, from the Ordovician of Colorado.
A cystoid echinoderm, a spiny ball on a short stalk, so abundant in the Middle Ordovician of Baltica that its skeletons form whole beds of limestone.
An actinocerid nautiloid whose chambers are threaded by a thick, beaded siphuncle -- common in the warm Middle Ordovician seas of North China and Laurentia.
The enrolled trilobite of the Cincinnati hills, found curled into a ball by the thousand; the commonest trilobite of Late Ordovician North America.
A smooth, rounded trilobite that lay half-buried in the sea floor with only its eyes showing -- common on the Ordovician shelves of Baltica.
The first tabulate coral: small colonies of prismatic tubes in Early Ordovician limestones of Laurentia and Siberia, before reefs had corals.
A two-metre, big-mouthed stem tetrapod with tiny forelimbs -- back in the water, an ambush hunter of the Mississippian lakes.
A metre-long tetrapod from Romer's Gap -- the stretch after the Devonian that had yielded almost no land vertebrates -- with feet that point forward, built for walking.
One of the earliest tetrapods, known from jaws and limb bones from the Late Devonian of Scotland -- a metre and a half long and still mostly in the water.
A Late Devonian stem tetrapod from Latvia, between Tiktaalik and Acanthostega -- probably with limbs, still with a fish's tail fin.
An early lungfish of the Middle Devonian lake of northern Scotland, whose crushing tooth plates are almost those of a living lungfish.
A lobe-finned fish of the Middle Devonian lagoons with a flat head, no dorsal fins and the beginnings of fingers in its fin bones.
An early tetrapod with eight fingers and internal gills -- limbs evolved in the water, not for walking on land.
A more robust tetrapod from East Greenland, able to haul itself but still tied to water.
taxa.hb: amphibious, with limbs but a fish-like tail

taxa.note: The 'fishapod': a three-metre lobe-finned fish with a neck, a flat head and fins with wrist bones, from Late Devonian river deposits now on Ellesmere Island.
A flat-headed predator with a neck, wrists and lungs, found in Arctic Canada exactly where and when the rocks predicted it would be.
The largest arthropod known: a sea scorpion some two and a half metres long, known from a 46-centimetre claw, hunting in Early Devonian estuaries.
An early vascular plant carrying sporangia along the sides of its stems, on the line that leads to the lycophytes.
An early lycophyte with leaf-like enations along a branching stem, and rooting structures that are not yet true roots.
A phacopid trilobite of the Devonian of Morocco and Bohemia, one of the enrolled trilobites quarried from the Anti-Atlas by the thousand.
A jawless fish with a streamlined armoured head shield ending in a long snout, and wing-like spines behind its head that steadied it as it swam.
A spiny 'shark' of the Old Red Sandstone of Scotland, a hand long, with paired rows of fin spines under its belly.
A Rhynie chert trigonotarbid preserved in such detail that its book lungs and leg joints can be counted.
Rhynie chert jaws of disputed affinity, argued to be the oldest insect -- possibly even a winged one.
From the Rhynie chert, and the earliest clear evidence of arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis - land plants have always been partly fungal.
taxa.hb: rootless, in a hot-spring wetland

taxa.note: A Scottish hot-spring deposit that silicified an entire Early Devonian land ecosystem where it stood.
A large solitary horn coral of the Middle Devonian whose fine growth ridges, counted as days, show about 400 days in a Devonian year.
A millipede from ~425 Ma Scotland with open spiracles -- the oldest direct evidence of an animal breathing air.
A stubby Silurian millipede of the earliest land litter, feeding on decaying plant matter beside water.
Scales and teeth from the late Silurian of Gotland and Russia that belong near the root of all bony fishes, four hundred and twenty-five million years old.
A metre-long Silurian sea scorpion with a broad body and a spiked tail, from the lagoons of southern Scotland.
A small anaspid of the Silurian of Lesmahagow and Norway, deep-bodied and scaled, with a tail that bent downward: an early jawless fish that swam in open water.
Chain coral, a diagnostic Silurian reef builder whose colonies form linked palisades.
taxa.hb: colonial reef builder, chain-like

taxa.note: A branching bryozoan whose colonies are dotted with star-shaped mounds; in the Cincinnatian it is a rock-forming fossil.
A colonial microbe, probably a cyanobacterium, whose Ordovician blooms made the kukersite oil shale of Estonia -- which still fuels the country's power stations.
A big, flat-coiled gastropod with a heavy lid, lying on the Ordovician sea floor like a stone -- its shells stud limestones from Tennessee to Scotland.
A long-lived conodont whose cone-shaped elements are in almost every Ordovician and Silurian limestone; the animal itself was a small eel-like swimmer.
A giant straight-shelled nautiloid, possibly six metres long, hunting the shelf seas.
taxa.hb: nektonic, with a long straight conical shell

taxa.note: A blind trilobite with three long spines, sometimes fossilised walking in single-file 'conga lines' across the sea floor.
A smooth Tremadocian asaphid of the cool Gondwanan shelves -- Argentina, Bolivia, Morocco, Bohemia, Wales -- and of Kazakhstan.
The conodont of the Cambrian-Ordovician boundary: its species define the last Cambrian and the first Ordovician zones on every continent.
The tuning-fork graptolite, two branches hanging from a float; a colonial drifter whose fossils zone the Early Ordovician worldwide.
A large late Cambrian trilobite of the Laurentian carbonate shelf, the zone fossil of the last Cambrian stage in North America from Wisconsin to Texas.
A tiny, blind agnostid trilobite, a few millimetres long and so widespread that it zones Cambrian rocks across several continents.
A broad trilobite the size of a hand from the late Cambrian sandstones of Wisconsin and Minnesota, the largest animal of the Laurentian shallows of its day.
The Laurentian trilobite of the Elvinia zone, the standard of the late Cambrian across the Great Basin and the Appalachian shelf.
The trilobite everyone has held: Elrathia kingii from Utah's Wheeler Shale, quarried by the million from a low-oxygen shelf it had almost to itself.
A smooth-shelled corynexochid of the Laurentian outer shelf, in the Burgess Shale, the Wheeler Shale and the limestones between them.
A radiodont with a long, hood-like carapace over its head -- first described piecemeal as several different animals.
A spiny trilobite of the middle Cambrian of Laurentia, its pleurae drawn out into long points, from the Wheeler Shale of Utah to the Rockies.
A scale-covered mat grazer whose affinities have been argued between molluscs and annelids for a century.
taxa.hb: benthic, armoured with sclerites and spines

taxa.note: A lancelet-like swimmer from the Burgess Shale with a notochord and V-shaped muscles: one of the oldest chordates.
A burrowing priapulid worm, the commonest predator of the Burgess Shale sea floor, found with hyoliths in its gut.
The 508-Ma community of British Columbia - the fullest window on Cambrian soft-bodied animals anywhere.
A velvet-worm-like lobopodian of the Burgess Shale, often found among the sponges it may have fed on.
A thirteen-centimetre Burgess Shale predator whose gut held crushed trilobites and hyoliths.
A spiny olenellid trilobite that defines the Laurentian faunal province of the Cambrian tropics.
taxa.hb: benthic

taxa.note: One of the commonest Burgess Shale arthropods: a bivalved, shrimp-like bottom-feeder that also lived in the Chengjiang sea.
A spined, stilt-legged lobopodian reconstructed upside-down and backwards for decades before anyone got it right.
taxa.hb: benthic walker

taxa.note: A gilled lobopodian of Sirius Passet with swimming flaps and two long, spined head limbs -- a snapshot of the step from lobopodians to arthropods.
Sponge-grade cone-shaped reef builders that made the first animal reef framework and were extinct within twenty million years.
A three-winged frond of the Nama assemblage, one of the last of the Ediacaran soft-bodied forms, surviving into the first million years of the Cambrian.
A segmented ribbon of the Gaojiashan biota of Shaanxi, a few centimetres long, pyritised in three dimensions: an animal of the last Ediacaran sea floor whose kind is still argued.
A tube of nested cones from the Gaojiashan biota of Shaanxi, pyritised and preserved whole: the organic-walled kin of Cloudina, and one of the first animals to build a tube to live in.
Fractal, self-similar fronds anchored in deep water at Mistaken Point -- a body plan with no modern counterpart.
Jawless fish with a solid bony head shield and sensory fields along its edges -- close relatives of the first jawed vertebrates.
Silurian Gotland is a fossilised barrier reef of tabulate and rugose corals and stromatoporoids.
A naked, eel-like jawless fish of the Lesmahagow Silurian of Scotland, with a ring of cartilage round its mouth: a lamprey's kin or something older.
A trinucleid trilobite with a broad, pitted fringe around its head -- a sieve for filtering food from the Late Ordovician mud.
A gumdrop-shaped trepostome bryozoan of the Trenton and Cincinnatian limestones, and of Baltica: the bryozoan that built the Late Ordovician sea floor's small mounds.
A large asaphid trilobite of the Baltic Ordovician, some species carrying their eyes on long stalks to see over soft mud.
The red 'Orthoceras limestone' of Sweden and Estonia is a graveyard of straight-shelled cephalopods.
A big asaphid trilobite of the Baltoscandian Ordovician, common in the orthoceratite limestones.
Two stipes folded back on themselves: the graptolite of the Dapingian, the Isograptus victoriae zones named from Victoria and found from Newfoundland to China.
Colonial corals built from stacked tubes with floors across them. Palaeozoic reef framework, extinct at the end-Permian.

The black Alum Shale of Scandinavia: olenid trilobites and agnostoids by the million in an oxygen-starved sea over Baltica, from the late Cambrian into the Ordovician, the source of the Furongian standard.
The late Cambrian trilobite of the Baltic alum shales, living in black oxygen-poor mud that preserved it in its thousands.
Alum-shale nodules of Sweden preserve millimetre crustaceans in uncrushed three-dimensional phosphate.
A smooth-shelled trilobite of the Jince beds of Bohemia and the Cambrian of Scandinavia, the first trilobite described from Bohemia (1825).
A tiny eodiscid with eyes, a spine on its head and a spine on its tail, of the middle Cambrian on every shelf from Laurentia to Australia.
A tiny eodiscid a few millimetres long with a serrated tail, of the early Cambrian of Avalonia, Siberia, Spain and Laurentia: small, blind and everywhere.
The large olenelloid of the Avalonian shelves -- the Brigus Formation of Newfoundland, the Comley limestones of Shropshire, the Braintree slates of Massachusetts -- Avalonia's own first trilobite.
A large olenellid trilobite of the early Cambrian Scandinavian shelf.
An olenellid trilobite of the early Cambrian Baltic and Laurentian shelves.
Calcareous tubes standing in dense stands on the earliest Cambrian shelves of Avalonia -- the Bonavista Peninsula, Massachusetts, Shropshire -- and Siberia.
One of the oldest trilobites of Baltica, from the earliest Cambrian shelly faunas.

A tommotiid of the Tommotian of Siberia and the Avalonian shelves of England and Newfoundland, known from its sclerites; a zone fossil of the stage that first showed the Cambrian had begun before the trilobites.
A quilted, vane-like Ediacaran organism of the terminal-Ediacaran Nama sandflats.
The Siberian crane, breeding on Arctic wetlands and wintering five thousand kilometres south.
Dahurian larch, the only tree that forms forest on continuous permafrost.
A low, ground-hugging birch of tundra and the ragged edge of the boreal forest.
The 'Siberian unicorn': a four-tonne steppe rhinoceros with a single enormous horn, which survived until about 39,000 years ago.
Golomyanka: translucent, scaleless Baikal fish, a third oil by weight, bearing live young in open water.
Bears. Omnivorous, wide-ranging, and one of the few large carnivores that hibernates through a boreal winter.
Antelopes, cattle, sheep and goats: hollow-horned ruminants that radiated with the spread of Old World grassland. Only a handful ever crossed to the Americas.
Cottongrass, whitening Arctic bogs in summer and building the tussocks of the tundra.
Bears: big omnivorous carnivorans of the northern continents, reaching South America with the interchange, where the spectacled bear is the last of the giant short-faced line.
A swan-necked lambeosaurine with a fan-shaped crest, from the very end of the Cretaceous on the Amur.
Squat, spiny-cheeked parareptiles a hand or two long. They crossed the end-Permian extinction and were everywhere in the Triassic.
The last forests before the Great Dying, buried under the largest volcanic eruption of the eon -- the coal seams of Tunguska are their remains.
Amphibians and early reptiles of the Permian rivers, the northern counterparts of the Karoo fauna.
Scorpions: among the first arachnids ashore, and scarcely changed in outline since the Carboniferous.
Wood-producing plants that still reproduce by spores -- the structural revolution before the reproductive one.
A Ludlow monograptid with paired spines on each cup, the zone fossil of the late Silurian shales of Wales, Bohemia and the Baltic.
The strawberry-headed trilobite of Silurian reef flanks, its head covered in tubercles, from Dudley and Gotland to Laurentia, Siberia and Australia.
Isolated on its own tropical craton, Siberia grows a distinctive Ordovician trilobite fauna.
Four stipes from one point, a Floian graptolite of the open ocean whose species date the early Ordovician worldwide.
A smooth-shelled trilobite of the late Cambrian of North China, Korea and Kazakhstan, the zone fossil of the Changshanian on the North China platform.
The big trilobite of the Burgess Shale, a hand long, preserved with its legs, gills and antennae: the animal that showed what a trilobite carried under its shield.
A Siberian trilobite of the Botomian stage, the zone fossil of the Lena and Aldan shelves in the middle of the early Cambrian.
The Siberian Platform yields the type Tommotian assemblage - the first mineralised skeletons, mostly millimetre tubes and spines.
taxa.hb: benthic, mostly millimetric

taxa.note: Siberia's first trilobite, from the lower Atdabanian of the Lena river: a fallotaspidoid at the very start of the Siberian trilobite record.
A bilaterally segmented, shield-shaped animal of the White Sea assemblage, one of the forms that made the Ediacaran seem an animal world.
A spiny odontopleurid whose long pleural spines swept back the length of its body: the emblem of the Ordovician Mediterranean province, from Bohemia and Morocco to Wales and Turkey.
The lace-collar trilobite: blind, with a pitted fringe around the head that filtered the mud it ploughed through.
The fringed trilobite of the Welsh Ordovician, blind, its pitted brim thought to sense currents in the mud it ploughed.
A single-stemmed graptolite with square-cut cups, the drifting plankton of Late Ordovician black shales on every continent.
Eel-like chordates known mostly from their tooth elements, which become the finest stratigraphic tool in the Palaeozoic.
A dicynodont of the Junggar Basin at the very end of the Permian, one of the tusked plant-eaters that were about to inherit the Earth.
A brachiopod so modified for reef life it looks like an oyster: cemented, with a comb of internal ridges; one of the odd forms of the Permian reefs of Texas and the Tethys.
A large spherical fusulinid foraminifer, up to a centimetre across, and an index fossil of the warm Permian Tethyan shelves.
A large Silurian brachiopod that formed dense shell banks across carbonate shelves.
A calymenid of the Armorican, Iberian, Bohemian and Moroccan Ordovician, found rolled up by the hundred in the quartzites of Brittany.
A blind cheirurid with a broad gently rounded shield, of the muddy cold-water shelves of Bohemia, Iberia, Morocco and Wales on the Gondwanan side of the Rheic Ocean.
The first graptolite to leave the sea floor: a conical net of branches hanging from a float, drifting over every Tremadocian sea.
Trilobites so different on its two shores that the contrast first revealed the ocean's former existence.
A half-metre gilled lobopodian of Sirius Passet, walking and swimming at once, with frontal claws -- a relative of the radiodonts.
Glass sponges building a reef belt along the Tethyan shelf larger than any reef system before or since.
A body plan with no counterpart in any living phylum.
taxa.hb: sessile, three-rayed symmetry

taxa.note: A flat, segmented, centimetre-to-metre oval that left feeding traces as it moved; cholesterol in its tissues shows it was an animal.
taxa.dt: external digestion of the mat beneath it
taxa.hb: flat on a microbial mat, possibly mobile

taxa.note: A bush-shaped rangeomorph, its fronds radiating from a common base rather than standing on a stalk.
A shark whose males carried an anvil-shaped fin on the back topped with a brush of tooth-like scales: display, most likely.
The goniatite that names its group: a globular ammonoid with zigzag sutures, a swimmer of Mississippian seas on every continent.
A six-metre placoderm that sheared prey with self-sharpening bony blades instead of teeth.
taxa.hb: nektonic apex predator with bladed jaw plates instead of teeth

taxa.note: A clymeniid ammonoid, its siphuncle on the inside of the coil, of the last Devonian stage: the group appeared and vanished within the Famennian.
An early shark from the Cleveland Shale, preserved with skin and muscle: a fast open-water hunter with the terminal mouth of a fish rather than a shark's underslung one.
A placoderm as long as Dunkleosteus but with no teeth: a filter-feeder, the first giant to make a living straining the sea.
A spiriferide brachiopod that spread almost worldwide in the Late Devonian, as the earlier provincial faunas merged.
The Late Devonian conodont whose platform elements zone the Frasnian and Famennian on every continent, and whose lineages thin out across the Kellwasser extinction.
A Late Devonian goniatite whose disappearance marks the Frasnian-Famennian extinction, one of the five great ones.
Colonial hemichordates drifting in open water, whose fast turnover makes them the timekeepers of the Ordovician.
A small, finely ribbed strophomenide lying flat on Ordovician and Silurian mud floors worldwide, often in shell beds by the thousand.
A small tongue-shaped phosphatic brachiopod of Cambrian and Ordovician shelves, burrowing like its living cousin Lingula.
Two stipes curving up like horns, the Late Ordovician graptolite of the black shales from Scotland to Kazakhstan and Australia.
A half-metre arthrodire placoderm of the Gogo reef, preserved in three dimensions in limestone nodules -- the state fossil of Western Australia.
A lobe-finned fish from the Gogo reef of Western Australia, preserved whole in three dimensions, with the wrist bones and nostrils of a fish on its way to land.
A calmoniid trilobite of the Malvinokaffric Realm, the cold Devonian shelves of Brazil, Bolivia and the Falklands, with spines and a raised tail.
A trilobite whose broad, hooked tail shield is the 'swallow stone' of Shandong, collected as a curiosity in China for a thousand years.
A damesellid trilobite with long spines fanning from its tail, typical of the Guzhangian seas of North China.
The Wheeler Shale of the House Range of Utah: Elrathia and Peronopsis by the thousand, and a Burgess Shale-type soft-bodied fauna in the deeper beds, the commonest trilobites ever sold.
Five eyes and a hose-like proboscis ending in a claw; the Burgess Shale animal that drew laughter when first described.
The commonest animal of the Burgess Shale, a thumbnail-sized arthropod with sweeping head spines; thousands of specimens, no close living relative.
A radiodont with pincer-like grasping claws, one of the top predators of the Chengjiang sea.
The trilobite of the Mount Stephen beds above Field, British Columbia, which lie thick with its moults: found before the Burgess Shale, and the reason Walcott came.
A trilobite of the Emu Bay Shale with more thoracic segments than almost any other -- over a hundred -- the record-holder among all trilobites.
A millimetre-sized bivalved bradoriid, the most abundant animal of the Chengjiang sea, sometimes preserved with eggs under its shell.
One of the oldest known vertebrates, from Chengjiang: a few centimetres long, with a head, gills and a notochord.
taxa.hb: nektonic

taxa.note: An arthropod of the Chengjiang sea whose brain and nerves were fossilised -- evidence that complex arthropod brains already existed in the Early Cambrian.
A jawless Cambrian fish-like chordate, preserved well enough to show its dorsal fin and segmented muscle blocks.
taxa.hb: nektonic, with a skull and rudimentary vertebral elements

taxa.note: The defining Cambrian arthropod: armoured, mobile, with compound eyes made of calcite crystals.
Archaeocyath reefs of the Shackleton Limestone in the Transantarctic Mountains: the Cambrian sea over the edge of East Antarctica, at the equator, building the first animal reefs beside Australia's.
The shallow sea records repeated sudden trilobite mass-extinctions and rebounds - the classic 'biomere' pattern.
A megacheiran arthropod with long, whip-tipped 'great appendages' in front, fossilised with its nervous system in the Chengjiang beds.
A soft-shelled, trilobite-like arthropod without eyes or a segmented back -- a naraoiid, common in both the Chengjiang and the Burgess seas.
Slender phosphatic spines with a rhombic cross-section, the sclerites of an unknown animal, whose first appearance marks Cambrian Stage 3 from Siberia and Avalonia to China and Australia.
Reindeer or caribou, the only deer in which both sexes carry antlers, grazing lichen through the northern winter.
The chamois, goat-antelope of the Alps, Carpathians and Caucasus.
Reindeer: the only deer where both sexes carry antlers, and the large herbivore that makes tundra a grazed system rather than a frozen one.
A seven-metre allosauroid, the top predator of the Barremian of the Isle of Wight; its snout was threaded with nerve canals, perhaps for sensing prey.
A pterosaur with a five-metre wingspan and a rounded beak edged with interlocking triangular teeth -- perhaps a scavenger.
A four-metre, long-armed, lightly built early tyrannosauroid -- a sketch of Tyrannosaurus sixty million years before it.
A chicken-sized coelurosaur dinosaur washed into the lagoon, its last meal a lizard in its gut.
A five-metre megalosauroid of the Callovian, found in marine clay near Oxford -- its body had drifted from one of the islands that Jurassic Europe was broken into.
A shrew-sized docodont of the Middle Jurassic lagoon shores, known from nearly complete skeletons from the Isle of Skye.
A rod-shaped stromatoporoid sponge that grew in dense thickets in the lagoons behind Devonian reefs.
A springtail from the Rhynie chert, ~410 Ma: the oldest known hexapod, and effectively a modern-looking one.
A leafless, rootless Rhynie chert plant preserved cell by cell, and the closest thing we have to a photograph of the first land ecosystem.
The black shales at the top of the Doushantuo Formation: carbonaceous seaweeds by the dozen, the spiral Eoandromeda, tubes and worm-like forms, a quiet late Ediacaran sea floor in South China.
A four-fold body with bundled fibres from the Fermeuse Formation of Newfoundland, read as the oldest animal with muscles: a stalked cnidarian.
A comb-shaped rangeomorph of Mistaken Point, a row of branches rising from a basal stolon, thousands preserved by volcanic ash on one surface.
A spindle-shaped rangeomorph of Mistaken Point, its self-similar branches all on one face, that lay flat on the deep-sea mud in the dark.
Shows evidence of reproduction by stolons.
taxa.hb: reclining on the sea floor, deep water

taxa.note: A triangular, cone-shaped organism of the Avalon deep sea floor, read by some as the oldest sponge.
A rangeomorph frond of the Drook Formation of Newfoundland, among the oldest large animals known at about 574 million years.
The Lantian Formation of Anhui: macroalgae and enigmatic soft-bodied forms in black shale just after the Marinoan ice, among the oldest large complex organisms.
Phosphatised spheres of dividing cells from the Doushantuo Formation of Guizhou, argued for twenty years to be animal embryos and by others to be giant bacteria or algae.

Simple discs and rings a centimetre across in the Twitya Formation of the Mackenzie Mountains, laid down between the two Cryogenian glaciations: the oldest candidates for the Ediacaran kind of large body, ten million years before the Marinoan ice.
A large acritarch with concentric striations, one of the longest-lived Proterozoic eukaryotes, in shales for nine hundred million years.
Testate amoebae from the Chuar Group and elsewhere - the oldest fossils of shelled, predatory eukaryotes.
The Svanbergfjellet Formation of Spitsbergen: Proterocladus and other green algae, acritarchs and cyanobacterial mats on the Tonian margin of Baltica.
A stalked, bulb-headed macroalga of the Tonian of North China, a few centimetres tall, held to the sea floor by a disc.
A branching green alga a few millimetres tall, from the Tonian of North China and Spitsbergen: the oldest known green seaweed, and green plants' first anchor to the sea floor.
A branching, budding microfossil of the Mesoproterozoic and Tonian, read by some as an early fungus, by others as an alga; either way, a complex cell a billion years before animals.
Branching filaments with chitin-like walls from Arctic Canada, and the strongest candidate for the oldest fungus.
A filamentous red alga with differentiated cells - among the oldest fossils tied to a living group.
taxa.hb: filamentous, attached to shallow substrate

taxa.note: A filamentous yellow-green alga of the Lakhanda Group of Siberia, close to the living Vaucheria; one of the first algae that can be placed in a modern group.
Alternating iron-rich and silica-rich layers precipitated from a ferruginous ocean. They largely stop forming by 1.85 Ga, once the deep sea holds oxygen.

Clusters of tiny cells packed into a mulberry-shaped colony, the commonest fossil of the Cryogenian interglacial shales on every continent; a cyanobacterium or a stressed eukaryote, either way the plankton of the seas between the snowballs.
A large spiny acritarch, the cyst of a Tonian eukaryote, found in shales from Siberia to Svalbard and Australia: the plankton of the world before the snowball.
An early hinged brachiopod of the late Cambrian, found on every continent's shelf, from a family near the root of the orthides.
A bilaterally symmetrical grazer that scraped mats with a feeding structure -- the best candidate for an early mollusc relative.
taxa.hb: mobile bottom-dweller

taxa.note: A small productid brachiopod with a ridged margin, on Permian sea floors from the Salt Range to Texas.
A spiny productid brachiopod that anchored itself in soft mud with hair-fine spines, a Permian shell of cool and warm seas alike.
A small ribbed athyridid brachiopod of late Palaeozoic shelves, from the Brazilian Permian to the Glass Mountains of Texas.
The 'scissor-tooth shark', with a single blade of teeth in each jaw that never shed; a Pennsylvanian predator the size of a great white.
Calcified sponges that are the principal reef framework builders of the Middle Palaeozoic.
'Devil's toenails' — thick curved oysters strewn across the Jurassic seabed of western North America.
