Stalked crinoids that rafted on driftwood over the open sea.
The fast-growing staghorn and table corals that build most of the framework of a modern reef.
A rudist bivalve grown into a tall cone with a lid, packed upright in thickets that built the reefs of the Late Cretaceous Tethys in place of corals.
Dugongs and manatees: the only plant-eating marine mammals, grazing seagrass meadows of warm shallow shelves.
A massive, slow-growing reef coral whose skeleton records annual bands like tree rings.
A flightless, toothed diving bird that swam the seaway like a loon.
taxa.hb: flightless foot-propelled diver, toothed

taxa.note: Thalassinoides: the branching burrow systems of shrimps and their forebears, a trace fossil that turns Cretaceous chalk and Jurassic limestone into a network of tunnels.
Tongue-shaped leaflets of the medullosan seed ferns, small trees whose fronds reached several metres; they are the commonest plant fossil in the ironstone nodules of the coal measures.
A climbing seed fern that hung on tree ferns and scale trees by hooked frond tips -- the lianas of the coal forests.
Leaflets joined at their bases in long, strap-like rows -- the foliage of Medullosa, a seed fern whose seeds could be as large as a hen's egg.
The Adelie penguin, nesting on the few ice-free Antarctic shores and feeding on krill under the pack.
As glossopteris but with non-midribbed leaves
taxa.hb: as Glossopteris but with non-midribbed leaves

taxa.note: Water bears, microscopic animals that survive freezing and drying alike; in Antarctica they are among the few permanent land animals.
Ferns. The understorey of every forest since the Carboniferous, and the whole canopy of some; for a few thousand years after the Chicxulub impact, fern spores are almost all there is.
A spiral graptolite throwing off side branches, the zone fossil of the Wenlock in Britain, Bohemia, Baltica and Arctic Canada.
Lacy, net-like bryozoans that built small reefs and meadows on Palaeozoic carbonate shelves.
The plain single-stiped graptolite that outlived the Hirnantian ice: Normalograptus persculptus names the last Ordovician zone and its kin the first of the Silurian.
A slender S-shaped graptolite whose first appearance defines the base of the Sandbian; found on every Late Ordovician shelf and ocean floor.
A late Cambrian trilobite with long genal spines and a narrow body, from Laurentia, Siberia, Kazakhstan, Australia and China; a zone fossil across the Jiangshanian.
A large flat trilobite of the middle Cambrian of Queensland and the Northern Territory, the zone fossil of the Australian Templetonian.
Australia's first trilobite: Abadiella huoi of the Flinders Ranges and the Stansbury basin, a redlichiid at the base of the Australian trilobite record.
The snow sheep, isolated on the range's high plateaus.
The brown bear, from Spanish mountains across Siberia to Alaska.
Mountain avens, the tundra mat-plant whose leaves in lake mud named the Younger Dryas cold snap.
Mountain sorrel, circling the Arctic and climbing every northern range, a first coloniser of raw ground.
A small segmented Ediacaran of the White Sea, a centimetre long, with the offset left-right quilting of Dickinsonia's kin; the genus that named the Vendian.
Organic-walled cysts of algae, too poorly understood to classify but abundant enough to date rocks with.
Stromatolite reefs of the Vazante Group on the Sao Francisco craton, columns and domes of a Tonian carbonate platform.
The Tonian Mbuji-Mayi Supergroup yields acritarchs and vase-shaped microfossils - genuine eukaryote fossils from the craton's cover.
A nine-metre early tyrannosauroid covered in long filament feathers -- the largest feathered animal known.
A two-metre early tyrannosauroid with a coat of protofeathers -- evidence that the tyrannosaur line was fuzzy from the start.
The Daohugou beds: Middle-Late Jurassic lake deposits with salamanders, feathered dinosaurs and the earliest gliding mammals.
The tropical coal-forest flora - Gigantopteris, Lobatannularia - that built the great Shanxi coals.
Bulky armoured herbivorous reptiles, the cattle of the terminal Permian landscape.
A spiny-tailed damesellid trilobite of the late Middle Cambrian of North China and Korea.
An eyeless conocoryphid trilobite, of Middle Cambrian seas from North China to Avalonia and Bohemia.
A Middle Triassic marine Lagerstatte in Yunnan documenting the recovery of ocean life after the extinction.
The Meishan section is the global boundary marker for the end-Permian extinction, in continuous marine limestone.
The lycopsid of the Xinhang forest of Anhui, the oldest forest known in Asia: thousands of trees preserved standing in a Late Devonian coastal swamp.
A crinoid that floated from a gas-filled bulb instead of rooting on the sea floor; drifting colonies of it cover whole bedding planes at the Silurian-Devonian boundary.
A long, straight-shelled nautiloid of the Late Ordovician of South China, whose sectioned shells make the 'pagoda stones' of Chinese decorative stone.
The commonest animal of the Emu Bay Shale of Kangaroo Island, a small trilobite preserved by the thousand, some with the bite marks of Anomalocaris.
An early Cambrian Lagerstatte in Yunnan, older than the Burgess Shale and just as detailed -- soft tissue, guts and nervous systems.

An eight-armed spiral a few centimetres across, in the Doushantuo shales of South China and the Ediacara sandstones of the Flinders Ranges: the same animal on two continents, and a candidate ctenophore.
Weng'an phosphorites preserving algae and controversial embryo-like fossils at cellular resolution, ~600 Ma.

Organic-walled microfossils and Bavlinella colonies in the manganese-bearing black shales of the Datangpo Formation of South China: life in the ten-million-year interglacial between the Sturtian and Marinoan ice.

Mineralised scales a few microns across, of a dozen shapes, from the Fifteenmile Group of the Yukon: the armour of Tonian eukaryotes, the first biomineralisation known, laid down in the shallow sea of Laurentia's western edge before the Sturtian ice.
The late Tonian shales of the Grand Canyon: vase-shaped amoebae, spiny acritarchs and the first sign of predation on eukaryotes, in a sea over Laurentia thirty million years before the ice.
A vase-shaped microfossil of the Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon: the shell of a testate amoeba, and among the oldest fossils that can be tied to a living eukaryote group.

The chert microfossils of the Bitter Springs Formation of central Australia: cyanobacterial mats, colonial cells and eukaryotic algae preserved cell by cell, the standard picture of a Tonian shallow sea.
A Silurian conodont, known from tooth-like elements a millimetre long that zone the Wenlock and Ludlow worldwide.
A peltasperm seed fern whose leaf, long called Callipteris, is the classic sign of the base of the Permian in the red beds of Europe -- a plant of drier ground than the coal swamps.
The largest insect known: a griffinfly with wings spanning 71 centimetres, which hunted other insects over the Early Permian coastal plain of Kansas.
An early conifer of the Glossopteris country, in Permian India and Australia, when conifers were still rare south of the tropics.
A peacock-sized oviraptorosaur with a fan of long feathers on its tail and short feathered arms -- a dinosaur built for display, not flight.
A two-metre therizinosaur with long, stiff filament feathers, among the first dinosaurs found with a feathery coat.
A perch-like predatory fish of the Green River lakes, sometimes preserved choking on its last meal.

The cherts and shales of the Atar and El Mreiti groups of the Taoudeni basin of Mauritania, about 1.1 billion years old: cyanobacterial mats, colonial cells and the cysts of early eukaryotes, on a shallow sea over the West African craton.
One of the oldest turtles with a modern-looking shell and jaw, from the Early Jurassic of Arizona.
The oldest known frog with the long hind legs and hips of a jumper, from the Early Jurassic of Arizona.
A beaver-sized tritylodontid, a plant-eating near-mammal; one was found with 38 babies -- a reptile-sized litter in an animal close to mammals.
A four-metre sauropodomorph with big clawed hands -- evidence that the early long-necks reached North America from the south more than once.
The largest ostrich-mimic, six metres long, built to outrun Tarbosaurus across the Nemegt floodplain.
The gemsbok, tolerating body temperatures that would kill most mammals.
The meerkat: a small mongoose of the Kalahari living in co-operative mobs with sentries.
The brown hyena, a shaggy scavenger of the Kalahari and the Namib coast, where it takes seal pups.
The ostrich: a flightless bird that answered open ground by running rather than hiding, and the largest bird alive.
Water-storing plants of arid ground -- cacti in the Americas, euphorbias and aloes in Africa and Arabia, two unrelated answers to the same problem. They spread as the deserts did, from about 30 Ma.
Hyenas began as civet-like tree-dwellers in Miocene Europe and became bone-crackers; one running form even reached North America.
Hyraxes look like marmots and are cousins of elephants. In the Eocene and Oligocene they were Africa's main herbivores, some the size of a small rhino.
The fennec fox, radiating heat through outsized ears.
The cheetah, fastest land animal, a sprinter of open ground.
The Laperrine's olive, a relict of wetter Sahara clinging to the massif's heights.
The date palm, the tree that makes an oasis: feet in groundwater, head in the desert sun.
The one-humped camel of Arabia and the Sahara, able to lose a third of its body water and drink it back in minutes.
Horses and zebras. Their high-crowned teeth and single toe are the standard example of an animal rebuilt by the spread of grass.
Spiny-tailed lizards: plant-eating desert agamids that block their burrows with a clubbed tail.
Gazelles: small, fast antelopes of open arid country from Morocco to India.
Camels -- which evolved in North America and only later reached the deserts they are now the emblem of.
The desert poplar, surviving on groundwater along dry river courses.
Jerboas: hopping desert rodents with kangaroo legs and tufted tails.
The wild Bactrian camel, drinking salt water no other large mammal tolerates.
The goitered gazelle of the Gobi and the Iranian plateau.
Saxaul: leafless, salt-tolerant small trees that are the only woodland the Central Asian deserts have.
The onager or kulan, the wild ass of the Asian deserts, able to run at 70 km/h.
The striped hyena, a solitary scavenger of dry country from the Sahel to India.
Beetles, cockroaches, dragonflies and the first true bugs of the Karoo's Permian, preserved as wings in the lake shales.
A turkey-sized feathered dromaeosaur of the Jehol forests; its fossils keep pigment cells that suggest reddish-brown and black plumage.
True crocodiles, alligators and gharials. Their range is a thermometer: they reached the Arctic in the Eocene and are tropical now.
Army ants whose swarm raids drive the understorey's whole insect economy.
The kapok, an emergent tree standing above the canopy with buttress roots metres tall.
Pebble toads endemic to individual tepui tops, which roll away from predators.
The American bison, whose herds shaped the whole grassland before 1870.
The pronghorn, still outrunning a predator that went extinct 12,000 years ago.
Blue grama, the shortgrass prairie's dominant sod-former.
Century plants: rosette succulents that flower once, on a mast several metres tall, and die.
Mesquite and algarrobo: thorny legume trees with taproots reaching tens of metres to groundwater.
The last North American camel, taller than a dromedary, gone around 11,000 years ago in the land where camels evolved.
The American badger, digging out ground squirrels across the prairie.
Open grassy country spreads as the world cools and dries after the Eocene, and grazing mammals begin evolving the tall, cement-filled teeth that silica-rich grass demands.
The saiga, its bulbous nose filtering dust and warming winter air.
The wild horse, the steppe's defining grazer.
The bobak marmot, whose burrowing turns over the steppe soil.
The argali, largest of wild sheep, its horns spiralling to nearly two metres.
The African bush elephant, whose feeding keeps the savanna from closing to woodland.
The blue wildebeest, whose migration is the largest surviving land-mammal movement.
The lion, the only truly social big cat.
The giraffe, browsing acacia crowns five metres up.
The plains zebra, migrating with the wildebeest.
The black rhinoceros, a hook-lipped browser of thorn scrub.
The gelada, the last grass-eating primate, endemic to these escarpments.
The Arctic fox, changing coat colour with the season.
Lemmings, whose population cycles drive the whole tundra food web.
Arctic willow, a centuries-old tree growing flat against the ground.
The snowy owl, a daytime hunter of lemmings on open tundra.
Woolly fringe-moss, the grey carpet over the lava fields of Iceland and Jan Mayen.
Purple saxifrage, flowering at the northernmost point of land on Earth.
The muskox, a survivor of the Pleistocene mammoth steppe.
Ptarmigan: grouse with feathered feet, white in winter and mottled in summer.
The woolly mammoth, keystone grazer of the mammoth steppe, surviving on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago.
taxa.hb: cold-adapted grazer of the mammoth steppe

taxa.note: The steppe bison, ranging the land bridge between continents.
The cave lion, hunting across Beringia's cold grassland.
The wild yak, dense-coated for the plateau's thin cold air.
The chiru, migrating hundreds of km across the plateau to calve.
The kiang, the wild ass of the Tibetan Plateau.
A spiny-tailed trilobite whose first appearance at Balang in Guizhou defines the base of the Wuliuan and the Miaolingian series, found from India and Siberia to Nevada.
A cheirurid trilobite with a swollen, globe-shaped head and long spines -- perhaps a swimmer in open water.
A thelodont preserved whole in the Silurian of Scotland: a flattened jawless fish with a forked tail and, unexpectedly, gill-pouch denticles.
A worldwide fungal spike of filaments and spores at the extinction horizon itself, usually read as the rot of a collapsing land flora, though some workers argue the fossils are algae.
A ten-metre megalosaurid, one of the largest predators of the Late Jurassic, on both sides of the young Atlantic; its eggs, with embryos inside, were found in Portugal.
The harpy eagle, taking sloths and monkeys out of the canopy.
The giant otter, two metres long, hunting Amazonian rivers in noisy family groups.
The black caiman, five metres long, the largest predator of the Amazon basin.
The capybara, the largest living rodent, grazing in herds at the water's edge.
An armoured, car-sized relative of armadillos, native to South America -- the interchange traveller into North America was its relative Glyptotherium.
A tapejarid pterosaur with an enormous sail-like head crest, taller than its skull was long.
A homalonotid trilobite of the Malvinokaffric Realm, heavy-shelled and adapted to cold siliciclastic bottoms.
Diagnostic of the cold high-latitude Gondwanan realm.
taxa.hb: benthic, cold-water shelf

taxa.note: The giant anteater, tearing open termite mounds with its foreclaws and feeding with a sixty-centimetre tongue.
The maned wolf, long-legged for seeing over cerrado grass.
The giant water lily, its ribbed leaves three metres across.
Fire-adapted savanna woodland with thick corky bark and vast root systems.
A bizarre caiman with a long, flat, duck-like snout, probably a filter-feeder straining small prey from the water.
American opossums: small omnivorous marsupials of South America, one of which has walked as far north as Canada.
The greater rhea of the pampas and cerrado.
Howler monkeys, whose dawn roar carries five kilometres through the forest.
The South American giant short-faced bear: early arrivals after the interchange may have stood three metres tall and weighed over a tonne.
The green anaconda, heaviest of all snakes, an ambush hunter of swamp and slow river.
Mahogany, the emergent timber tree of the Neotropical forest.
The one notoungulate to leave South America, a rhino-sized grazer that reached Texas in the Great American Interchange.
Macaws, the great long-tailed parrots that gather at riverbank clay licks.
Chinchillas of the high, dry Andes, carrying the densest fur of any land mammal.
The huemul, a stocky Andean deer of the southern forests.
The guanaco, wild ancestor of the llama, from sea-level Patagonian steppe to the high Atacama.
A cushion plant that builds hard green mounds a metre across on windswept subantarctic fellfield.
Creosote bush and jarilla: resinous desert shrubs of both Americas, whose clonal rings in the Mojave are among the oldest living things.
The western gorilla, a folivore of dense secondary forest.
The okapi, the giraffe family's last forest-dwelling member, confined to the Ituri rainforest of the Congo.
Papyrus sedge, forming floating swamps along African rivers and lake margins.
The Nile perch, a two-metre predator of the Nile, Chad and Congo systems.
The Nile crocodile, top predator of African rivers and lakes.
The darter, a spear-fishing bird of warm fresh waters that swims with only its snake-like neck above the surface.
Desert antelope able to let their body temperature rise through the day rather than spend water cooling it.
A phacopid trilobite with a long three-pronged trident on its head, perhaps used by males in contests.
A large, flat asaphid trilobite of Avalonia and the Gondwanan margin -- the 'Welsh trilobite', the first trilobite ever figured in print, in 1698.
An early Cambrian trilobite of the West Gondwanan shelves, and the marker of the Bigotinid province.
The critically endangered Saharan cheetah, ranging vast arid territories.
The hippopotamus, whose nightly paths and wallows engineer the channels of African wetlands.
The shoebill, ambushing lungfish in papyrus swamp.
The African buffalo, in herds of a thousand on the floodplains.
The camel thorn, the Kalahari's great shade tree, rooted sixty metres down.
The chimpanzee, our closest living relative, a tool-maker of forest and forest edge.
The marsupial mole, blind and swimming through sand.
Mulga, the wattle whose upswept leaves funnel rain to its own trunk; it covers a fifth of the continent.
A flightless bird twice the weight of an emu, whose eggshell in human campfires helps date people's arrival.
The Komodo dragon, a three-metre monitor that evolved in Australia and survives on a few Indonesian islands.
Flat-topped thorn trees, browsed to their characteristic silhouette by giraffe.
Wombats: burrowing marsupial grazers with ever-growing teeth.
The moose: the largest deer, browsing willow and feeding in boreal lakes and bogs.
The common loon or great northern diver, nesting on northern glacial lakes and wintering at sea.
The lake trout, a cold-water char of the deep glacial lakes left by the Laurentide ice.
The dwarf willow, a tree a few centimetres tall, creeping through Arctic and alpine snowbeds.
Peccaries, the New World's answer to pigs: North American for thirty million years, South American only since the land bridge.
Red oat grass or kangaroo grass, the fire-adapted dominant of savannas from Africa to Australia.
The wandering albatross, with the widest wingspan of any living bird, circling the Southern Ocean between breeding seasons.
The Portuguese man o' war, a colony of specialised animals sailing under a gas-filled float.
Swarming eyeless vent shrimp that crowd Atlantic and Indian Ocean chimneys, farming bacteria on their shells.
Vent mussels living on sulphur-eating bacteria in their gills — no sunlight, no photosynthesis.
Albatrosses, gliding the wind belts for years between landfalls on remote islands.
Giant tube worms up to 2 m long, mouthless and gutless, fed by symbiotic bacteria — icons of the 1977 vent discovery.
Sea-floor sediment made of siliceous diatom skeletons, under the high-productivity belts of the Southern Ocean and the North Pacific.
Big white clams clustered in the warm sulphide flow around vents and seeps, fed by chemosynthetic bacteria in their gills.
The whale shark, the largest fish alive, filtering plankton at the surface of warm seas.
Tropicbirds, plunge-divers of the warm open ocean that nest on the remotest islands.
Marlins and sailfish, the fastest fishes of the open tropical ocean.
The sooty tern, which stays on the wing for years at sea and breeds in vast colonies on tropical islets.
The northern fulmar, a cold-water petrel that nests on sea cliffs from Brittany to the High Arctic.
The Greenland shark, the longest-lived vertebrate known; individuals are thought to reach four centuries.
The harp seal, whelping on the pack ice of the North Atlantic and following the ice edge through the year.
The little auk, nesting by the million in High Arctic scree and wintering on the open North Atlantic.
The Atlantic cod, the fish that fed and built the North Atlantic's coasts, from the Grand Banks to Lofoten.
The king penguin, breeding in colonies of hundreds of thousands on the subantarctic islands.
The southern elephant seal, bulls of four tonnes hauling out on subantarctic beaches to fight and breed.
Eaton's pintail, a small duck found only on Kerguelen and the Crozet Islands.
Kerguelen cabbage, a wind-pollinated crucifer of the subantarctic islands; whalers ate it against scurvy.
A tussock grass of Kerguelen, Heard and Marion Islands, thickest where seals and penguins manure the ground.
The greater burnet of the far south, carpeting sheltered slopes from Patagonia to Kerguelen.
The Weddell seal, the southernmost mammal, keeping breathing holes open in fast ice with its teeth.
Petrels, shearwaters and storm-petrels: tube-nosed seabirds that come ashore only to breed.
Long-necked, four-flippered marine reptiles that 'flew' underwater, from coastal forms to open-ocean giants.
Dolphin-shaped marine reptiles, from one to over twenty metres, bearing live young at sea from the Early Triassic on.
Modern sharks. Their constantly shed teeth are the commonest vertebrate fossils of many shallow seas.
Beaked whales, the deepest-diving mammals: Cuvier's beaked whale has been logged at nearly three kilometres.
The dugong, the one strictly marine sea cow left, grazing seagrass from the Red Sea to the Coral Sea.
A branching reef coral of the Indo-Pacific; its Red Sea populations tolerate unusually hot water.
The giant clam: up to 1.3 m and 250 kg, fixed for life on an Indo-Pacific reef and fed largely by the algae it farms in its own mantle.
Butterflyfishes, coral-pickers whose numbers rise and fall with the reef itself.
A Late Cretaceous belemnite whose bullet-shaped guards fill the Maastricht chalk; its oxygen isotopes were among the first used to read past sea temperatures.
The Mauritian flying fox, the island's last native mammal and the pollinator of its forest trees.
The Mauritius kestrel, reduced to four wild birds in 1974 and brought back by captive breeding.
Day geckos, bright green nectar-feeders that spread from Madagascar to every island group of the western Indian Ocean.
Mauritius ebony, the black-hearted timber the Dutch cut the island's forests for.
Latan palms, a fan-palm genus confined to the Mascarenes, one species to each island.
The tambalacoque, long and wrongly said to need the dodo's gut to germinate; a slow canopy tree of Mauritius.
The dodo, a giant flightless pigeon of Mauritius, extinct within a century of the first ships.
The giant tortoises of Mauritius, Reunion and Rodrigues, five species grazing in herds of thousands until the 1700s.
The top predator of Late Cretaceous Madagascar -- a short-snouted abelisaur whose tooth marks on its own kind are clear evidence of cannibalism.
A pug-nosed, plant-eating crocodile relative from Madagascar, less than a metre long and armoured like an armadillo.
The 'devil frog': a 40 cm horned frog relative from Madagascar, big enough to take hatchling dinosaurs.
The polar bear, a brown-bear offshoot that became a marine mammal, hunting seals from the sea ice.
The Aldabra giant tortoise, last of the Indian Ocean's giant tortoises, a hundred thousand strong on one atoll.
Seychelles frogs, thumbnail-sized, whose nearest relative lives in India: they have ridden these granite islands since the two parted.
The Seychelles fruit bat, roosting by the hundred in the islands' takamaka and breadfruit trees.
The Seychelles black parrot, a few hundred birds in the palm forest of Praslin.
The coco de mer of Praslin, bearing the largest seed of any plant, up to twenty-five kilograms.
The Seychelles pitcher plant, on bare granite summits; an early offshoot of a genus otherwise centred on Borneo.
The jellyfish tree of Mahe, sole member of its lineage, thought extinct until a few dozen were found in the 1970s.
The grey mangrove, the most salt- and cold-tolerant of all, fringing desert coasts from the Red Sea to New Zealand.
Antarctic icefish carrying antifreeze glycoproteins in their blood, a radiation that tracks the freezing of the Southern Ocean.
The yellow-eyed penguin, nesting alone in coastal forest rather than in colonies.
The kea, the world's only alpine parrot, and one of its cleverest birds.
Kiwi: nocturnal, flightless, nostrils at the tip of the bill, laying an egg a fifth of their own weight.
The tuatara, last of the sphenodontians, with a 'third eye' on top of its head and a life span over a century.
Rimu, the weeping podocarp that towers over New Zealand's lowland rainforest.
The silver fern, a tree fern whose fronds shine white beneath.
Kauri, the giant of the northern New Zealand forest, its trunks five metres through.
Haast's eagle, the largest eagle known at up to 15 kg, which preyed on moa and died out with them.
Giant weta: flightless crickets heavier than a sparrow, filling the role mice play elsewhere.
Moa: nine species of wingless birds, the largest 3.6 m tall, that were New Zealand's browsers in place of mammals until about 1400 CE.
The kakapo: flightless, nocturnal, the heaviest parrot, breeding only when the rimu trees mast.
New Zealand's native frogs: no eardrums, no croak, no tadpoles -- little changed since the Jurassic.
A Chinese dinocephalian therapsid: the Cathaysian block's own big Middle Permian predator, on a landmass separated from the rest.
The klipspringer, a small antelope that walks on the tips of its hooves on bare rock.
The mountain zebra of the Cape ranges and the Namibian escarpment.
The giant panda, a bear turned bamboo specialist. In the Pleistocene it ranged from Beijing to Vietnam and Burma.
The golden snub-nosed monkey of the Qinling, living through snowbound winters on lichen and bark.
The dove tree, a relict of the Tertiary forests of the northern hemisphere surviving in the mountains of Sichuan.
A pot-bellied, ten-metre plant-eating theropod with the longest claws of any animal -- up to a metre each.
A fifteen-to-twenty-metre sauropod with a neck of seventeen vertebrae, one of the mamenchisaurids that kept East Asia's giants distinct while it was cut off from the rest of Pangaea.
A massive brontothere with a forked nasal horn, abundant in the White River badlands and extinct by the mid-Oligocene.
The saguaro: a column cactus of the Sonoran Desert that takes seventy years to grow its first arm.
The Joshua tree of the Mojave, pollinated by a single species of moth; its seeds were once spread by ground sloths.
A small plant of the Rhynie hot-spring marsh with a lumpy underground corm and a spore capsule with a central column like a moss's -- from before the vascular plants settled their plan.
The babirusa of Sulawesi, whose upper tusks grow up through the snout and curl back toward the skull.
The anoa, a dwarf forest buffalo barely a metre tall, found only on Sulawesi.
The rainbow gum, the only eucalypt native north of the equator, its bark peeling in green, orange and purple strips.
The helmeted muskox, a taller, woodland relative of the living muskox, found only in Ice Age North America.
The woolly rhinoceros, its appearance known from cave paintings as well as bones.
The muskox, a survivor of the Pleistocene mammoth steppe that rings its calves with horns against wolves.
The Malayan tapir, black and white, the only Old World tapir left.
Teak, the great timber tree of the monsoon forests, leafless through the dry season.
The great hornbills, seed-dispersers of the Asian rainforest, the female sealed into the nest hole.
The saltwater crocodile, largest living reptile, crossing open sea between estuaries.
The wild boar, ploughing forest floors from Portugal to Japan.
Giant rosette lobelias of the Afroalpine moorland.
The kosso tree of the African mountain forests, up to the edge of the moorland.
The big roaring cats: lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar. Ambush predators that track the large herbivores of each continent.
True elephants and mammoths, with washboard grinding teeth built for grass. African in origin; mammoths carried the family to the Arctic and to Mexico.
Snakes: limbless lizards that swallow prey whole. They diversify after the Cretaceous, alongside the small mammals they eat.
Solitary and colonial Palaeozoic corals, extinguished entirely; the corals that follow are a different lineage.
Stalked echinoderms in meadows so dense that entire limestone formations are made of their debris.
A shark relative with a buzzsaw whorl of teeth in its lower jaw, whose function took a century to work out.
taxa.hb: nektonic, with a spiral tooth whorl in the lower jaw

taxa.note: The Mazon Creek 'Tully monster' -- eyes on a bar, jaws on a proboscis, and no settled classification.
A thirty-centimetre shark of the Bear Gulch lagoon; males carried a spine curving forward over the head like a sickle, used, it seems, in courtship.
Marine reptiles with flat crushing teeth and, in some, turtle-like armour, specialised on shellfish.
A thin-shelled bivalve that paves the black, oxygen-poor shales of Jurassic Europe -- the 'Posidonia Shale' -- by the million.
Robust ark clams, common on sandy sea floors from the Jurassic onward.
'Lago Mare' phase — brackish Paratethyan mussels flooding a Mediterranean nearly emptied and freshened before the Atlantic broke back in.
Bacteria and archaea living in lakes sealed beneath four kilometres of ice, without light, on minerals ground from the bedrock.
Hundreds of cichlid species evolved inside single African lakes -- in Lake Victoria, in perhaps fifteen thousand years.
The beluga sturgeon of the Caspian and Black Sea basins, up to a tonne and a century old.
The Titicaca grebe, flightless and found on this one lake system.
The queen of the Andes: a bromeliad that grows for eighty years at 4,000 m, flowers once on a ten-metre spike, and dies.
The lesser flamingo, filtering cyanobacteria from soda lakes caustic enough to burn skin.
The stag-moose: a moose-sized deer with elaborate palmate antlers, living in the spruce bogs at the ice margin.
The giant deer or 'Irish elk', carrying antlers 3.6 m across -- the largest of any deer.
The golden eagle, hunting open mountain country around the whole northern hemisphere.
The bezoar or wild goat of the Zagros and Taurus, ancestor of the domestic goat.
The common wombat, a burrowing grazer with a backward-facing pouch.
The emu, nomadic across the whole continent, walking hundreds of kilometres after rain.
Wombat-like browsers that reached rhinoceros size -- the largest marsupials ever.
A dog-sized marsupial lion of the Miocene rainforests of Queensland, with blade-like premolars for slicing meat.
A stocky titanosaur from the Winton Formation of Queensland, found beside the predator that may have fed on it.
A lightly built six-metre megaraptoran with huge hand claws: Australia's best-known predatory dinosaur.
Australia's most complete dinosaur: a sheep-sized armoured ankylosaur preserved with its last meal of ferns and fruit.
An eight-metre Australian ornithopod with an inflated, hollow snout -- probably for calling across the polar forests.
A Cretaceous monotreme known from an opalised jaw at Lightning Ridge -- platypus relatives are at least this old.
A small, big-eyed ornithopod from Dinosaur Cove, which lay inside the Antarctic Circle: it lived through months of winter darkness.
A corynexochid with a spiny pygidium of the Cambrian shelves of Laurentia, Siberia and Australia, common in the Burgess Shale and the limestones around it.
Snow tussocks, the tall bunch grasses of the New Zealand high country.
The Gila monster, a venomous lizard that spends nine tenths of its life underground.
The blue mussel, a Pacific native that crossed into the Atlantic when the Bering Strait opened.
The oldest undisputed member of the modern bird groups: a relative of ducks and geese from the last of the Cretaceous in Antarctica, with a voice box that could honk.
A barrel-shaped rudist, one of the strange bivalves that grew in thickets and built the reefs of the Late Cretaceous tropics in place of corals.
Colonial encrusters and branching forms that build much of the reef and hardground framework.
The 'Pompeii worm', living on chimney walls in some of the hottest water any animal endures.
The mara: a long-legged, hare-like cavy of the Patagonian scrub that pairs for life.
Globular cacti of the Atacama coast that live on fog: some stands see no rain for decades.
A rootless air plant forming banded 'lawns' on bare Atacama dunes, watered entirely by coastal fog.
The largest-headed bird known: a terror bird with a 71 cm skull, running down prey on the Miocene Patagonian plain.
The Arabian oryx, white against the sand; extinct in the wild by 1972 and returned from captive herds.
The frankincense tree of Dhofar and Somalia, growing from bare rock and bled for its resin for five thousand years.
The pichi, a small armadillo of cold Patagonian steppe and the only one known to hibernate.
Neneo, the spiny cushion shrub that dots the wind-scoured Patagonian steppe.
The Arctic hare, white year-round in the far north, gathering in flocks of hundreds.
A long-snouted tyrannosaur with a row of bony bumps along its nose -- a slender cousin of the giant Tarbosaurus.
A solid-crested duckbill found on both sides of the Late Cretaceous land bridge across the Bering region, in Alberta and in Mongolia.
A mouse-sized multituberculate of the Gobi dunes -- one of the rodent-like mammals that outnumber all others in the Late Cretaceous.
The Siberian musk deer: antlerless, with sabre-like canines.
The Mongolian gazelle, still migrating in herds of tens of thousands across the eastern steppe.
A hornless dinocerate with a big, bulbous snout, from the Middle Eocene of Mongolia.
Found on a nest in 1923 and named 'egg thief', it was later shown to be brooding its own eggs -- a toothless, beaked oviraptorosaur of the Gobi dunes.
A metre-long, fast, bipedal plant-eater with pointed front teeth -- possibly an omnivore -- from the forests of the Jehol.
An emu-sized oviraptorid known from adults sitting on their nests, arms spread over the eggs like a brooding bird, smothered by sand where they sat.
Schrenk's spruce, which forms the dark forest belt on the north slopes of the Tien Shan.
Giraffe relatives were once spread from Spain to China, many of them short-necked and moose-like; the giraffe and okapi are the African remnant.
A sparrow-sized enantiornithine of the Barremian wetlands -- one of the 'opposite birds' that were the commonest birds of the Cretaceous.
An early ostrich-dinosaur with more than 200 tiny teeth, the most of any theropod, and a throat pouch preserved in the rock.
A six-metre carcharodontosaurid with a strange tall hump over its hips, raised on two lengthened vertebrae.
The 'wonderchicken': the oldest skull of a modern bird, a quail-sized relative of both chickens and ducks from the last Cretaceous shores of Europe.
A six-toed Devonian tetrapod from the Tula region of Russia, with limbs strong enough to walk on the bottom.
The heavyweight of the Morrison plain -- a massively built diplodocid with a neck as deep as a horse's body.
The Ethiopian wolf, Africa's rarest carnivore, hunting Afroalpine rodents.
Giant groundsels, tree-sized daisies of the East African summits, each mountain with its own species.
A two-metre early theropod from New Mexico -- one of the fossils showing that dinosaurs spread north from southern Pangaea within a few million years of their origin.
The perentie, Australia's largest living lizard at over two metres, a hunter of the rocky deserts.

n.15: A ground sloth from the northward spread of South American mammals via the new Panama land bridge.
n.43: A hypercarnivorous creodont, the leading predator of the Oligocene plains.
n.52: Dawn-redwood swamp forest ran across the warm Eocene interior and up onto Ellesmere Island, inside the Arctic Circle.
n.63: A rhino-sized herbivore with six blunt horns and sabre canines from the Bridger Basin.
n.80: A tiny archaic primate relative from just after the K-Pg impact - among the first of our own order.

n.160: A six-tonne ground sloth the size of an elephant - the giant Darwin puzzled over in Patagonia.
n.169: Palm-dominated swamp across the Miocene Pebas mega-wetland that filled western Amazonia, the cradle of its modern diversity.
n.184: The endemic ungulate radiation continuing through the Oligocene isolation.

n.238: Fungus farmed in gardens inside African termite mounds, an agriculture tens of millions of years older than our own.
n.244: An early tool-making human from Olduvai Gorge, at the base of our own genus.
n.245: A robust, massive-jawed hominin ('Nutcracker Man') sharing the Pleistocene rift with early Homo.
n.247: The Laetoli trackway in Tanzania records these hominins walking bipedally through volcanic ash.
n.251: 'Lucy' and her kin - upright-walking hominins of the Pliocene East African savanna.
n.253: A large proboscidean with down-curved lower tusks, browsing the Miocene woodlands.
n.255: C4 grasses spread across Africa after about eight million years ago, turning closed woodland into open savanna: the habitat shift that frames human origins.
n.261: An early ape from Miocene East Africa, from the radiation that led to living apes and us.
n.270: A key early anthropoid from the Fayum of Egypt, near the root of monkeys and apes.
n.82: Mangrove-palm swamp fringed the Tethyan coast of Africa. The Fayum primates lived in forest right at the water's edge.
n.281: A fully aquatic early whale, 18 m of serpent-bodied predator, from the Eocene sea that covered Egypt -- the Valley of the Whales is full of them.
n.122: A fire- and drought-tolerant tree fern that carpeted the Cretaceous North African floodplains where Spinosaurus and Paralititan lived.

n.253: A giant hook-tusked proboscidean ranging the Pikermian savannas of the Miocene.
n.340: A hornless rhino the size of a small crane - the largest land mammal ever, from the Oligocene of Asia.
n.37: 'Hell pigs', massive omnivorous artiodactyls of the Oligocene Asian steppes.
n.207: Palm fronds and crocodiles at fifty degrees north. Messel preserves a paratropical forest in what is now Germany.
n.350: A huge flightless bird of the Eocene forests of Europe, once cast as a predator, likely a browser.
n.365: Flowering plants spreading through Laurasian forests, taking over from conifers and cycads in under thirty million years.
n.384: An early beaked bird from the Jehol lakes, found in the thousands, the males with a pair of long ribbon tail feathers.
n.385: A badger-sized Cretaceous mammal, one specimen with a juvenile dinosaur in its stomach -- mammals were not only prey.
n.388: The first dinosaur found with feathers -- a coat of simple filaments, and preserved pigment showing a ginger-and-white banded tail.
n.288: Ginkgo and its relatives at their peak across Laurasia, in a diversity now reduced to one surviving species.
n.399: From the Solnhofen lagoon: feathered, clawed and toothed, and for 150 years the single most argued-over fossil in the world.
n.448: One of the first really large dinosaurs, in bone beds across Germany, Switzerland and France -- dozens of individuals buried together in Triassic floodplain mud.
n.451: A reptile whose neck was longer than the rest of it -- three metres of it, with only twelve vertebrae -- fishing from Triassic shorelines.
n.462: A conifer of the Triassic river plains, part of the flora that recolonised Europe after the end-Permian coal gap.
n.467: A long-necked marine reptile of the Muschelkalk sea that flooded central Europe, hunting from the shore the way a seal does.

n.483: A three-tonne wombat relative, the largest marsupial ever to live.
n.486: A seven-metre monitor lizard (Megalania), Australia's largest land predator until the megafauna vanished.
n.487: The marsupial lion, with bolt-cutter premolars and the strongest bite for its size of any known mammal.
n.490: The Chinchilla Sand records the Pliocene shift from rainforest to open woodland as Australia dries.
n.193: Eucalypts and charcoal rise together through the Miocene record: fire and increasing aridity remaking a rainforest continent.
n.496: A toothed platypus from the Riversleigh limestones, showing the monotreme lineage's deep past.
n.187: Cool-temperate southern beech rainforest covered Australia before it dried. Its pollen dominates Eocene cores from the coast to the interior.

n.190: Rock-clinging lichens, the dominant life of ice-free nunataks.
n.187: Southern beech - the Seymour Island floras show Eocene Antarctica was cool temperate rainforest, not ice.
n.289: Monkey-puzzle relatives form the high-latitude woodland; body-fossils of its animals are scarce in this interval.
n.286: Southern-conifer forests clothe a warm-temperate Jurassic-Cretaceous Antarctica, still joined to the rest of Gondwana.

n.526: The Asian elephant lineage and a rich Siwalik-derived mammal fauna occupy the subcontinent.
n.535: A large proboscidean of the Miocene-Pliocene Siwalik faunas.
n.335: A great ape of the Siwalik foreland forests shed from the rising Himalaya.
n.354: Early bats among the exceptional Eocene mammals of the Cambay lignites as India nears Asia.

n.553: Filter-feeding baleen whales diversify to exploit booming plankton in the cooling seas.
n.561: Calcareous nannoplankton continue to floor the ocean with their microscopic plates.
n.566: The largest macropredatory shark ever, hunting whales across the Neogene ocean.
n.577: A serpentine early whale, fully marine at last, cruising the warm Eocene seas.
n.580: Diatoms radiate into a dominant plankton group, seeding rich cool-water food webs.
n.598: Ammonites remain the dominant open-ocean predators until their end-Cretaceous extinction.
